case: A 57-year-old female without any medical history was admitted for evaluation of a left ventricular tumor that was discovered incidentally. The patient was asymptomatic and had no relevant past medical history. Physical examination findings were not specifically described in the case report.

Left ventricular myxoma.description: A benign primary cardiac tumor usually found in the left atrium but rarely arising in the left ventricle; it may cause obstruction, embolic events, or be discovered incidentally.

Papillary fibroelastoma.description: A small benign cardiac tumor that commonly arises from valves or endocardial surfaces and may be found incidentally, although it can cause embolic complications.

Left ventricular thrombus.description: A blood clot within the left ventricular cavity, most often associated with prior myocardial infarction, reduced ventricular function, cardiomyopathy, or atrial fibrillation.

Cardiac lipoma.description: A benign tumor composed of mature fat that can occur in the myocardium, endocardium, or pericardium and is frequently asymptomatic unless large or strategically located.

Cardiac sarcoma.description: A rare malignant primary cardiac tumor that may arise in any cardiac chamber, including the left ventricle, and can cause obstruction, arrhythmias, heart failure, or systemic symptoms.

case: A previously healthy 10-year-old boy presented with left upper quadrant abdominal pain that worsened with deep breathing or lying down, accompanied by fever. He also complained of mild cough and whitish sputum. On physical examination, the child was irritable but there were no other remarkable findings. Laboratory data showed elevated C-reactive protein (8.65 mg/dL) without leukocytosis and other findings were unremarkable.

Left lower lobe pneumonia with pleurisy.normalized_text: Left lower lobe pneumonia with pleurisy
Left lower lobe pneumonia with pleurisy.description: Infection of the lower left lung that can irritate the pleura, causing abdominal or upper-quadrant pain rather than prominent chest symptoms in children.

Acute pleuritis.description: Inflammation of the pleural lining around the lungs, commonly caused by viral or bacterial respiratory infection, producing sharp pain with breathing or movement.

Viral lower respiratory tract infection.description: A viral infection involving the airways or lungs that may cause fever, cough, sputum production, pleuritic discomfort, and inflammatory marker elevation without leukocytosis.

Splenic abscess.description: A rare localized infection within the spleen that can cause fever, left upper quadrant pain, and elevated inflammatory markers; pain may worsen with breathing because of diaphragmatic irritation.

Subphrenic abscess.description: A collection of infected fluid beneath the diaphragm that may produce fever, upper abdominal pain, cough, and pleuritic pain due to irritation of the diaphragm and adjacent pleura.

case: A 38-year-old woman presented with a three-day history of fever, generalized myalgia and arthralgia, and the sensation of difficulty when breathing in. She had poorly localized discomfort in the left diaphragmatic region on deep inspiration and loose stools over the preceding three days. Three days before presentation she had returned from a three-week trip to Western Australia, and 18 months earlier she had traveled to Vietnam. On examination she appeared well but was febrile at 38.0°C and tachypnoeic at 22 breaths/min, with all other observations normal. Examination of all other systems was unremarkable. Blood tests showed severe neutrophilia (18.9 × 10⁹/L; reference range 2.0-8.1), raised C reactive protein (354 mg/L; reference value <10), and normal renal and liver biochemistry. Chest radiography and urinalysis were normal. Blood cultures taken at presentation were negative.

Acute Q fever (Coxiella burnetii infecti.description: A zoonotic bacterial infection acquired from exposure to livestock, animal birth products, or contaminated dust. It can cause an acute influenza-like illness, atypical pneumonia, hepatitis, or both; it occurs in Western Australia.

Legionnaires' disease (Legionella pneumo.description: A bacterial pneumonia acquired from contaminated water aerosols, including hotel plumbing, cooling systems, spas, and showers. It commonly causes fever, myalgia, gastrointestinal symptoms, and respiratory complaints.

Melioidosis (Burkholderia pseudomallei i.description: An infection caused by an environmental soil and water bacterium endemic in northern Australia. It can present with acute pneumonia, sepsis, localized infection, or nonspecific febrile illness.

Leptospirosis.description: A bacterial zoonosis acquired through contact with water or soil contaminated by urine from infected animals. It often causes abrupt fever, severe myalgia, headache, gastrointestinal symptoms, and occasionally pulmonary disease.

Influenza or another acute viral respira.normalized_text: Influenza or another acute viral respiratory syndrome
Influenza or another acute viral respira.description: Acute viral infections such as influenza can cause fever, generalized aches, arthralgia, respiratory discomfort, and gastrointestinal symptoms, sometimes before clear respiratory findings develop.

case: A 60-year-old white Caucasian woman presented with a 4-year history of worsening gait and sensory disturbance accompanied by urinary urgency and nocturia. She reported slow deterioration in vision from age 50, though she could still drive. Her mother was registered blind and had Parkinson's disease with dementia. On examination, she had a spastic gait with normal power in lower limbs but increased tone and sustained ankle clonus. Reflexes were brisk with flexor plantar responses. She had mild reduction in visual acuity and dyschromatopsia, but no detectable visual field defect and preserved pupillary light reflexes. CSF analysis showed presence of oligoclonal bands. Routine hematological, biochemical and immunological blood tests were normal, including folate and vitamin B12. Anti-aquaporin 4 antibodies were negative in serum.

Primary progressive multiple sclerosis.description: A progressive inflammatory demyelinating disorder of the central nervous system that can cause gradually worsening spastic paraparesis, sensory symptoms, bladder dysfunction, and optic pathway involvement.

Leber hereditary optic neuropathy-multip.normalized_text: Leber hereditary optic neuropathy-multiple sclerosis overlap syndrome (Harding disease)
Leber hereditary optic neuropathy-multip.description: A mitochondrial DNA-associated disorder in which Leber hereditary optic neuropathy occurs together with an MS-like inflammatory demyelinating syndrome, often including myelopathy, spasticity, sensory symptoms, and bladder dysfunction.

Hereditary spastic paraplegia with optic.normalized_text: Hereditary spastic paraplegia with optic neuropathy (for example SPG7-related disease)
Hereditary spastic paraplegia with optic.description: A group of inherited neurodegenerative disorders characterized by progressive lower-limb spasticity and urinary dysfunction; complicated forms can include optic atrophy, visual impairment, sensory symptoms, and ataxia.

OPA1-related dominant optic atrophy plus.normalized_text: OPA1-related dominant optic atrophy plus syndrome
OPA1-related dominant optic atrophy plus.description: A mitochondrial disorder caused by OPA1 variants, usually producing progressive bilateral optic neuropathy and sometimes additional neurologic features such as spasticity, neuropathy, ataxia, deafness, or movement disorders.

Adrenomyeloneuropathy in a female ABCD1.normalized_text: Adrenomyeloneuropathy in a female ABCD1 variant carrier
Adrenomyeloneuropathy in a female ABCD1.description: An X-linked peroxisomal disorder in which female carriers may develop a slowly progressive myelopathy resembling hereditary spastic paraplegia, with leg stiffness, sensory symptoms, and bladder dysfunction.

case: A 14-year-old female patient presented with generalized pruritus accompanied by scleral icterus and petechiae/ecchymoses on the extremities for over 2 months. She had no fever, abdominal pain, or distension. Past medical history included amenorrhea, menstrual irregularities, and acne. She had been taking Chinese herbal medicines (specific components unknown) for approximately 9 months. Physical examination revealed clear consciousness, facial acne and pigmentation, mild scleral and mucocutaneous jaundice, soft abdomen without tenderness or rebound tenderness, and no lower extremity edema.

Herb-induced liver injury (drug-induced.description: Liver injury caused by Chinese herbal medicines or supplements, often presenting with cholestasis, jaundice, itching, and impaired clotting.

Autoimmune hepatitis.description: An immune-mediated inflammatory liver disease that commonly affects females and may cause jaundice, itching, and liver-related coagulation abnormalities.

Wilson disease.description: An inherited disorder of copper accumulation that can cause hepatitis, jaundice, hemolysis, and progressive liver failure in children and adolescents.

Cholestatic viral hepatitis.description: Hepatitis caused by viruses such as hepatitis A, B, E, Epstein-Barr virus, or cytomegalovirus can occasionally produce a cholestatic presentation with marked itching and jaundice.

Biliary obstruction or intrahepatic chol.description: Impaired bile flow from obstruction of the bile ducts or intrahepatic cholestasis causes accumulation of bilirubin and bile acids, producing itching and jaundice.

case: 66-year-old man with a 2-day history of fever, lethargy, polyarticular arthralgias, and a painful rash. Medical history included hypertension, poorly controlled type 2 diabetes, hypercholesterolemia, and biopsy-proven autoimmune hepatitis; azathioprine 75 mg had been started 10 days earlier. On examination, he was febrile (38°C) with bilateral tender knees and a patellar tap. Labs showed leukocytosis with neutrophilia, elevated CRP and ESR, mildly elevated rheumatoid factor, and negative anti-CCP, dsDNA, ENA, and anti-ASO tests. Renal function and urinalysis were normal, chest radiograph was normal, and synovial fluid was noninflammatory with no bacteria or crystals.

Azathioprine hypersensitivity syndrome.description: An acute systemic hypersensitivity reaction to azathioprine, often occurring within days to weeks of starting therapy. It can cause fever, malaise, rash, arthralgia, neutrophilic leukocytosis, and elevated inflammatory markers.

Drug-induced Sweet syndrome (acute febri.normalized_text: Drug-induced Sweet syndrome (acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis)
Drug-induced Sweet syndrome (acute febri.description: A neutrophilic inflammatory skin disorder characterized by abrupt fever, painful tender erythematous skin lesions, neutrophilia, and elevated inflammatory markers. It may be triggered by medications, including azathioprine.

Serum sickness-like reaction.description: A medication-related immune reaction causing fever, rash, and polyarthralgia, typically developing one to three weeks after exposure to a new drug. Unlike true serum sickness, complement abnormalities and immune-complex disease may be absent.

Adult-onset Still disease.description: A systemic autoinflammatory disorder that can present with high fever, inflammatory arthritis or arthralgia, rash, neutrophilic leukocytosis, and markedly elevated inflammatory markers.

case: A 60-year-old woman presented after sustaining direct trauma to the anterior neck from a fall. She developed progressively worsening hoarse voice, difficulty swallowing, and pain with neck movement. Physical examination revealed visible neck swelling with bruising tracking onto the anterior chest wall. There was no tenderness on palpation of the cervical spine. On flexible nasal endoscopy, swelling of the posterior pharyngeal wall was observed, indicating potential airway compromise.

Retropharyngeal hematoma due to blunt ne.normalized_text: Retropharyngeal hematoma due to blunt neck trauma
Retropharyngeal hematoma due to blunt ne.description: Accumulation of blood in the retropharyngeal space after trauma, which can expand and threaten the upper airway.

Blunt laryngeal trauma with laryngeal ed.normalized_text: Blunt laryngeal trauma with laryngeal edema or hematoma
Blunt laryngeal trauma with laryngeal ed.description: Injury to the larynx from external neck trauma that may cause swelling, bruising, vocal cord dysfunction, airway narrowing, and voice changes.

Laryngeal fracture.description: Fracture of the thyroid or cricoid cartilage after blunt trauma, potentially causing hoarseness, swallowing difficulty, pain, neck swelling, and airway obstruction.

Traumatic pharyngeal hematoma.description: Bleeding within the pharyngeal soft tissues after blunt trauma, causing posterior pharyngeal swelling, painful swallowing, voice changes, and possible airway narrowing.

Cervical soft-tissue hematoma from vascu.normalized_text: Cervical soft-tissue hematoma from vascular injury
Cervical soft-tissue hematoma from vascu.description: A hematoma in the neck soft tissues caused by injury to cervical blood vessels following trauma; expansion can produce dysphagia, hoarseness, bruising, and airway compression.

case: 37-year-old man with 3 months of episodic weakness, irritability, poor concentration, craving sweets, foggy sensorium, cold/clammy feeling, fatigue, and memory/behavior changes, worse after several hours առանց food and at night/early morning. He gained 30 lb from drinking large amounts of cola for symptom relief. He had a similar presentation several days earlier. Past history was unremarkable except for umbilical hernia repair and back surgery 10 years earlier; no medications, no tobacco or illicit drugs, social alcohol use, and family history of diabetes. On examination he was confused, cold, and clammy; other system exams were unremarkable. Routine labs, HbA1c, adrenal testing, calcium/PTH, and pituitary/thyroid hormones were normal except mildly elevated prolactin. MRCP showed a 1.8 × 1.3 cm hypervascular slightly exophytic lesion anterior to the pancreatic head/neck.

Insulinoma.description: A usually benign pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor that secretes insulin inappropriately, causing recurrent fasting hypoglycemia (Whipple triad).

Endogenous hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia.normalized_text: Endogenous hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia due to pancreatic nesidioblastosis
Endogenous hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia.description: Diffuse overgrowth or hyperfunction of pancreatic beta cells causing excessive insulin secretion and recurrent hypoglycemia, usually without a discrete insulinoma.

Factitious hypoglycemia from exogenous i.normalized_text: Factitious hypoglycemia from exogenous insulin use
Factitious hypoglycemia from exogenous i.description: Hypoglycemia caused by intentional or accidental administration of insulin, typically producing neuroglycopenic and adrenergic symptoms during low blood glucose episodes.

Sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycemia.description: Hypoglycemia caused by medications that stimulate pancreatic insulin release, including accidental ingestion, medication error, or surreptitious use.

Adrenal insufficiency.description: Insufficient cortisol production can impair glucose maintenance during fasting and may cause fatigue, weakness, and hypoglycemia, especially during illness or prolonged fasting.

case: A 39-year-old male, with no prior relevant medical history, presents with atraumatic intermittent sharp pain in the lower segment of the right anterior thoracic wall. The symptoms began two months earlier when the patient started exercising (CrossFit), mostly triggered by training (especially abdominal crunches) whilst being asymptomatic in normal daily activities.

Intercostal muscle strain.description: Overuse or minor injury of the muscles between the ribs, commonly caused by intense exercise, twisting, or forceful core movements.

Rectus abdominis or upper abdominal wall.normalized_text: Rectus abdominis or upper abdominal wall muscle strain
Rectus abdominis or upper abdominal wall.description: Strain of the abdominal musculature near its attachment to the lower ribs or sternum, often occurring with repetitive abdominal exercises.

Costochondritis.description: Inflammation of the cartilage connecting the ribs to the sternum, causing localized anterior chest wall pain that may worsen with movement or exertion.

Slipping rib syndrome.description: Hypermobility of the lower false ribs, usually ribs 8 to 10, which can irritate intercostal nerves and produce intermittent sharp lower chest or upper abdominal pain with movement.

Xiphodynia (xiphoid syndrome).description: Pain arising from irritation of the xiphoid process or adjacent xiphosternal structures, sometimes precipitated by repetitive strain, abdominal exercise, or minor unrecognized trauma.

case: A 31-year-old woman underwent barium enema examination as part of a medical checkup. She had been healthy without specific complaints and had no significant past medical or family history. The patient was 161 cm in height and weighed 44 kg, appeared well, and the physical examination showed no abnormalities. Complete blood cell count and biochemical analysis of the blood for hepatic and renal function, urine analysis, and fecal occult blood test were all within normal limits. The tumor markers for CEA and CA 19-9 were also normal. No lesions were observed on the upper endoscopy and the abdominal ultrasound.

No apparent gastrointestinal disease.description: The available history, examination, laboratory tests, fecal occult blood test, tumor markers, upper endoscopy, and abdominal ultrasound do not identify a specific illness.

Asymptomatic colorectal polyp.description: A colorectal polyp is a growth from the lining of the colon that may be found incidentally during screening or imaging; many polyps cause no symptoms.

Early colorectal neoplasm.description: Early-stage colorectal cancer or another colonic neoplasm can occasionally be detected incidentally before symptoms or laboratory abnormalities develop, although it is uncommon at age 31.

case: A 67-year-old previously healthy male presented with a 4-month history of dry cough, wheezing, and mild dyspnea that had initially been diagnosed as eosinophilic asthma at another hospital, with symptoms worsening despite treatment with inhaled bronchodilators and corticosteroids. He had no smoking history and unremarkable medical history. On examination, he required 1L nasal cannula oxygen with SaO2 of 96%, had decreased breath sounds in the right lower lung field with fine crackles, and no raised JVP, murmurs, gallop, or peripheral edema. Chest x-ray showed right ground glass opacities, and high-resolution CT revealed ground glass opacities surrounded by consolidation in the right lower lung field.

Cryptogenic organizing pneumonia.description: An inflammatory lung disease characterized by organizing inflammation in distal airways and alveoli, often causing subacute cough, dyspnea, and patchy ground-glass or consolidative opacities. A reverse-halo pattern may be seen on CT.

Chronic eosinophilic pneumonia.description: A pulmonary eosinophilic disorder causing weeks to months of cough, dyspnea, wheezing, and pulmonary infiltrates; it is often associated with adult-onset asthma and responds to systemic corticosteroids.

Invasive mucinous adenocarcinoma of the.normalized_text: Invasive mucinous adenocarcinoma of the lung
Invasive mucinous adenocarcinoma of the.description: A subtype of lung adenocarcinoma that can spread along alveolar spaces and mimic pneumonia, producing persistent ground-glass opacities and consolidation with cough, dyspnea, and occasional wheezing.

Eosinophilic asthma.description: A type of asthma driven by eosinophilic airway inflammation, commonly causing wheezing, cough, dyspnea, and variable airflow limitation.

case: A 12-year-old boy presented with a 1-month history of malaise, fevers, abdominal pain, and worsening pallor. His symptoms began with headache and abdominal pain, with an initial temperature of 38.6°C and pale skin. He experienced persistent upper abdominal pain and recurrent fevers. The patient reported nausea, occasional diarrhea, headache, myalgias, fatigue, and occasional dizziness. He described nearly constant periumbilical pain radiating to the left lower quadrant, with occasional blood in stools. His height was 132 cm (1st percentile), weight 26.8 kg (1st percentile), with recent 1 kg weight loss. Physical examination revealed pale skin and mucosa, distended abdomen with mild tenderness in right upper and left lower quadrants, and ecchymoses on the shins. He had visited the Dominican Republic 3 months prior. Laboratory tests showed severe microcytic anemia (hemoglobin 6.7 g/dL), elevated inflammatory markers (ESR >140 mm/hr, CRP 143.2 mg/liter), and elevated ferritin (320 μg/L).

diagnoses.name: Mixed-cellularity subtype of classic Hodgkin's lymphoma
diagnoses.normalized_text: Mixed-cellularity subtype of classic Hodgkin's lymphoma

Crohn disease.description: A chronic inflammatory bowel disease that can affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract and commonly causes abdominal pain, diarrhea, anemia, weight loss, growth failure, and systemic inflammation in children.

Ulcerative colitis.description: A chronic inflammatory bowel disease limited to the colon that causes colonic inflammation, bloody diarrhea, abdominal pain, anemia, fever, and impaired growth in children.

Visceral leishmaniasis.description: A parasitic infection transmitted by sand flies in endemic regions, including parts of the Caribbean, that may cause prolonged fever, malaise, weight loss, anemia, abdominal enlargement from liver or spleen enlargement, and low blood cell counts.

Acute lymphoblastic leukemia.description: A childhood blood cancer involving immature lymphoid cells in the bone marrow. It can cause anemia, fever, fatigue, bruising, bone pain, abdominal symptoms, and increased susceptibility to infection.

Enteric fever (typhoid or paratyphoid fe.description: A systemic bacterial infection caused by Salmonella Typhi or Paratyphi, usually acquired through contaminated food or water during travel. It can cause prolonged fever, headache, abdominal pain, diarrhea or constipation, malaise, and occasionally gastrointestinal bleeding.

case: A 39-year-old man presented to the emergency department during the summer with a 4-day history of fever with shaking chills, diffuse headache, and fatigue following his return from a 2-week trip to East Africa. During his trip to Tanzania, he had been on safari without animal contact but received mosquito bites, especially during the first days. He consumed cooked shrimp and lobster and a small amount of raw tuna. On the second-to-last day of the trip, he developed nausea, vomiting, and nonbloody diarrhea. Upon returning to Massachusetts, he experienced fever (38.3°C to 39.5°C), shaking chills, diffuse headache, and lower back pain. He reported weakness, anorexia, decreased urine output with dark urine, and blurry vision during fever episodes. His medical history included degenerative knee disease with previous glucocorticoid injections. On examination, he had a temperature of 38.9°C, blood pressure 113/62 mm Hg, facial flushing, mild scleral icterus, and dark brown urine.

Plasmodium falciparum malaria.description: A severe mosquito-borne malaria caused by Plasmodium falciparum, common in East Africa and capable of causing high fevers, hemolysis, jaundice, kidney injury, and neurologic or visual symptoms.

Leptospirosis.description: A bacterial zoonotic infection caused by Leptospira species, often acquired through exposure to water or soil contaminated with animal urine. Severe disease can cause jaundice, kidney dysfunction, dark urine, headache, and fever.

Dengue fever.description: A mosquito-borne viral illness found in tropical regions that commonly causes abrupt high fever, severe headache, fatigue, muscle or joint pain, nausea, and sometimes rash or bleeding manifestations.

Enteric fever (typhoid or paratyphoid fe.description: A systemic bacterial infection caused by Salmonella Typhi or Paratyphi, usually acquired through contaminated food or water during travel. It can cause prolonged fever, headache, abdominal symptoms, anorexia, and fatigue.

Acute viral hepatitis, including hepatit.normalized_text: Acute viral hepatitis, including hepatitis A or E
Acute viral hepatitis, including hepatit.description: Acute inflammation of the liver caused by hepatotropic viruses, commonly acquired through contaminated food or water during travel. It may cause fever, malaise, nausea, anorexia, jaundice, and dark urine.

case: 24-year-old male with quadriplegia from a car accident 5 years prior that required cervical spine stabilization with metal plates. Presented with dysphagia, odynophagia, neck pain, fever, and chills. Medical history significant for quadriplegia requiring cervical spine stabilization with metal plates. CT and MRI showed large paraspinal abscess extending from cervical spine 4 to thoracic spine 11.

Spinal epidural abscess.description: A collection of purulent material in the epidural space around the spinal cord, often associated with vertebral infection or prior spinal procedures and capable of causing neurologic compromise.

Cervicothoracic paraspinal abscess.description: A bacterial infection producing a pus collection in the paraspinal soft tissues adjacent to the cervical and thoracic spine; it may extend over multiple vertebral levels and can occur after trauma, surgery, or hematogenous spread.

Cervical vertebral osteomyelitis with di.description: Infection and inflammation of vertebral bone and adjacent intervertebral discs, which can spread into paraspinal tissues and form epidural or paraspinal abscesses.

Delayed cervical spinal hardware infecti.description: Infection involving implanted cervical plates or other fixation hardware, potentially occurring years after surgery and leading to surrounding soft-tissue infection, osteomyelitis, and abscess formation.

Retropharyngeal or prevertebral abscess.normalized_text: Retropharyngeal or prevertebral abscess with extension to paraspinal tissues
Retropharyngeal or prevertebral abscess.description: A deep neck-space infection located behind the pharynx or in front of the cervical spine that can cause painful swallowing and may extend along fascial planes toward the mediastinum or paraspinal region.

case: A 58-year-old male with worsening nausea for the past 72 hours presented to the emergency department with severe chest pain radiating to the back in the context of 4 recent episodes of non-bloody, non-bilious emesis. He was afebrile, diaphoretic, and mildly tachycardic. Cardiac workup, complete blood count, and electrolytes were normal.

Boerhaave syndrome (spontaneous esophage.description: A full-thickness tear of the esophagus, most often caused by forceful vomiting, leading to leakage into the mediastinum and potentially life-threatening mediastinitis.

Mallory-Weiss tear.description: A mucosal tear at the gastroesophageal junction caused by retching or vomiting, typically resulting in upper gastrointestinal bleeding.

Acute aortic dissection.description: A tear in the inner lining of the aorta that allows blood to separate the layers of the aortic wall, classically causing abrupt severe chest pain that may radiate to the back.

Acute coronary syndrome.description: Myocardial ischemia caused by reduced coronary blood flow, including unstable angina and myocardial infarction; it can present with chest pain, sweating, nausea, and vomiting.

Acute pancreatitis.description: Inflammation of the pancreas, commonly causing severe upper abdominal pain that radiates to the back along with nausea and vomiting.

case: 27-year-old man with 2-year history of recurrent convulsive episodes. Initial events were shaking of the trunk, arms, and legs lasting 4–5 minutes, preceded by occipital pain radiating to the neck, blurred vision, palpitations, nausea, and difficulty concentrating. Four months before admission, he had an episode of sudden stiffening and fall backward with shaking for 5–8 minutes and urinary incontinence. Despite levetiracetam, he continued having seizures about weekly; one month before admission he was found on the floor with shaking and clenching movements lasting about 2 minutes. On examination, he was awake and alert but mute, with a stiff posture and intermittent nonrhythmic tremulous movements of the trunk and limbs. Notable history included childhood febrile seizure, several concussions, asthma, major depressive disorder, chronic PTSD, and panic disorder with agoraphobia. He had extensive burn scars on the face, trunk, back, arms, and legs. Basic laboratory tests were normal except mildly elevated lactate and creatine kinase.

Functional neurological symptom disorder.normalized_text: Functional neurological symptom disorder with attacks or seizures (psychogenic nonepileptic seizures, PNES)
Functional neurological symptom disorder.description: Seizure-like episodes caused by functional brain-body mechanisms rather than epileptic electrical discharges. They are often associated with psychological trauma, anxiety, depression, or PTSD and may include prolonged, variable, or nonrhythmic movements.

Generalized tonic-clonic epilepsy.description: A type of epileptic seizure involving loss of consciousness, generalized body stiffening followed by rhythmic jerking, and often a postictal period of confusion or fatigue.

Focal epilepsy with focal-to-bilateral t.normalized_text: Focal epilepsy with focal-to-bilateral tonic-clonic seizures
Focal epilepsy with focal-to-bilateral t.description: Epileptic seizures beginning in one brain region and potentially spreading to both sides of the brain, producing generalized stiffening and convulsions. Focal warning symptoms can precede the convulsion.

Catatonia.description: A neuropsychiatric syndrome characterized by abnormal motor behavior and changes in speech or responsiveness, including mutism, rigidity, posturing, negativism, agitation, or repetitive movements. It can occur with mood disorders, trauma-related disorders, psychosis, or medical illness.

Convulsive syncope.description: Brief loss of consciousness from reduced blood flow to the brain, sometimes accompanied by brief stiffening or jerking movements that can resemble an epileptic seizure. It may be associated with palpitations, visual disturbance, nausea, or other presyncopal symptoms.

case: 92-year-old woman with BMI 14.2 kg/m². Past history: no abdominal surgery, five children by normal vaginal delivery. Presenting with: 2-day history of sudden onset right knee pain, 1-day history of nausea and vomiting. Physical exam: no knee swelling/tenderness, patient frequently flexed right knee for pain relief, abdominal distension present, tenderness to deep palpation but no peritoneal irritation signs, no abdominal mass. Rectal exam revealed small extraluminal mass on right side. Initial abdominal radiograph showed small-bowel obstruction.

Obturator hernia with small-bowel obstru.description: A rare pelvic hernia in which bowel protrudes through the obturator canal. It classically occurs in thin, elderly, multiparous women and may cause bowel obstruction with referred medial thigh or knee pain due to obturator nerve compression.

Incarcerated femoral hernia causing smal.normalized_text: Incarcerated femoral hernia causing small-bowel obstruction
Incarcerated femoral hernia causing smal.description: A femoral hernia occurs when abdominal contents pass through the femoral canal below the inguinal ligament. In elderly women it has a high risk of incarceration and strangulation, potentially producing bowel obstruction.

Incarcerated inguinal hernia causing sma.normalized_text: Incarcerated inguinal hernia causing small-bowel obstruction
Incarcerated inguinal hernia causing sma.description: An inguinal hernia occurs when bowel or other abdominal contents protrude through the inguinal canal. If trapped, it can cause acute small-bowel obstruction and may progress to ischemia.

Small-bowel obstruction due to internal.normalized_text: Small-bowel obstruction due to internal hernia
Small-bowel obstruction due to internal.description: An internal hernia is protrusion of bowel through an intra-abdominal opening, which can cause obstruction and bowel strangulation. It may occur without prior abdominal surgery, although it is less common in this setting.

Small-bowel volvulus.description: Small-bowel volvulus is twisting of the small intestine around its mesentery, leading to mechanical obstruction and potentially bowel ischemia. It often causes acute abdominal pain, vomiting, and distension.

case: 23-year-old Korean female with 6 months of recurrent bilateral visual field defects and headache, worsening 1 month before presentation. She presented with 1-day left eye visual disturbance and visual field defect, then developed sudden left-sided hearing loss 2 days later. Three weeks after initial presentation, she reported right eye visual field defect, followed 2 days later by tinnitus, severe headache, and arm numbness. She denied significant past medical history, pregnancy, or oral contraceptive use. Examination showed reactive pupils without relative afferent pupillary defect, visual acuity 20/20 right and 20/25 left, normal intraocular pressure, and normal anterior segment findings. Laboratory studies were unremarkable, including normal lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin antibody, ESR, and CRP. CSF showed mildly elevated protein without oligoclonal bands.

Susac syndrome.description: A rare autoimmune microangiopathy affecting small vessels of the brain, retina, and inner ear. It classically causes branch retinal artery occlusions with visual field loss, sensorineural hearing loss, and encephalopathy or severe headache.

Multiple sclerosis.description: A chronic inflammatory demyelinating disease of the central nervous system that can cause recurrent neurologic deficits, including optic neuritis, sensory symptoms, and brainstem-related hearing or balance symptoms.

Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder.description: An autoimmune inflammatory disorder, often associated with aquaporin-4 antibodies, that mainly causes severe optic neuritis and longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis.

Cogan syndrome.description: A rare autoimmune inflammatory disease characterized by audiovestibular dysfunction, especially sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus, together with inflammatory eye disease such as interstitial keratitis or uveitis.

Antiphospholipid syndrome with retinal o.normalized_text: Antiphospholipid syndrome with retinal or cerebral ischemia
Antiphospholipid syndrome with retinal o.description: An autoimmune prothrombotic disorder that can cause arterial or venous thrombosis, including retinal vascular occlusions and cerebral ischemic events causing visual or sensory deficits.

case: 73-year-old woman with a 10-year history of severe paraspinal muscle atrophy and cerebellar ataxia. Symptoms began at age 63 with slight stooping posture, then progressive gait instability requiring a walking stick by age 68 and difficulty climbing stairs by age 70. Exam showed moderate neck flexion weakness, mild proximal limb weakness, poor balance with impaired tandem gait, and no limb ataxia. MMSE was 25/30. Labs showed elevated creatine kinase, normal blood and CSF lactate, low TSH, elevated antithyroglobulin and antithyroid peroxidase antibodies, elevated rheumatoid factor, and mildly elevated antinuclear antibody. Needle EMG showed mild myopathic changes. Audiometry revealed sensorineural high-frequency hearing loss, and Holter monitoring showed frequent premature contractions.

Mitochondrial myopathy with cerebellar a.normalized_text: Mitochondrial myopathy with cerebellar ataxia and sensorineural hearing loss
Mitochondrial myopathy with cerebellar a.description: A mitochondrial disorder causing progressive muscle weakness and atrophy, elevated creatine kinase, ataxia, hearing impairment, and sometimes cardiac rhythm abnormalities. Blood and CSF lactate can be normal in adult-onset mitochondrial disease.

MERRF-spectrum mitochondrial disease (my.normalized_text: MERRF-spectrum mitochondrial disease (myoclonic epilepsy with ragged-red fibers spectrum)
MERRF-spectrum mitochondrial disease (my.description: A mitochondrial DNA disorder, often associated with MT-TK variants, that can cause myopathy, ataxia, hearing loss, elevated creatine kinase, and cardiac involvement. Some adult cases have incomplete presentations without classic seizures or myoclonus.

POLG-related mitochondrial disease.description: POLG gene disorders are mitochondrial DNA maintenance disorders that may present in adulthood with ataxia, myopathy, hearing loss, neuropathy, seizures, ophthalmoplegia, or cardiac manifestations. The clinical spectrum is broad and may be incomplete.

Myofibrillar myopathy (for example, desm.normalized_text: Myofibrillar myopathy (for example, desmin-related myopathy or myotilin-related myopathy)
Myofibrillar myopathy (for example, desm.description: Myofibrillar myopathies are inherited or sporadic muscle disorders characterized by progressive axial, paraspinal, neck, and proximal limb weakness, elevated creatine kinase, and myopathic EMG findings. Desmin-related disease can also involve cardiac conduction abnormalities.

Late-onset Pompe disease.description: Late-onset Pompe disease is a lysosomal glycogen-storage myopathy that causes slowly progressive axial and proximal muscle weakness, paraspinal muscle involvement, neck flexor weakness, and difficulty climbing stairs. Creatine kinase may be mildly elevated.

case: A 2-year-old Korean male was admitted for evaluation and management of left hip pain. Physical examination revealed several palpable lymph nodes in the left inguinal area and an ill-defined heterogeneous mass-like lesion in the left anteromedial muscle. Peripheral blood examination showed hemoglobin 9.6 g/dL, white blood cell count 6.83 × 10^9/L, platelet count 182 × 10^9/L, and 5 atypical lymphocytes per 100 white blood cells. Immunophenotyping of neoplastic cells showed positivity for CD45 (99.0%), CD19 (94.84%), CD10 (27.64%), CD20 (94.24%), HLA-DR (95.70%), surface IgG lambda (96.45%), CD13 (22.46%), and CD117 (22.22%), and negativity for CD34 (0.01%), Tdt (0.64%), myeloperoxidase (0.01%), and various T-cell and myeloid markers.

diagnoses.name: B-cell lymphoma, unclassifiable, with features intermediate between diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and Burkitt lymphoma
diagnoses.normalized_text: B-cell lymphoma, unclassifiable, with features intermediate between diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and Burkitt lymphoma
diagnoses.icd11_title: B-cell lymphoma unclassifiable with features intermediate between Burkitt lymphoma and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma

Mature B-cell lymphoma/leukemia.description: A group of aggressive mature B-cell neoplasms that can involve lymph nodes, blood, bone marrow, and extranodal sites such as muscle. The strong surface immunoglobulin light-chain restriction and mature B-cell markers support this category.

Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL), p.normalized_text: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL), possibly with leukemic involvement
Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL), p.description: DLBCL is an aggressive mature B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma that may present with rapidly enlarging nodal or extranodal masses and can occasionally involve peripheral blood or bone marrow.

Burkitt lymphoma/leukemia.description: Burkitt lymphoma is a highly aggressive mature B-cell lymphoma of childhood. It commonly expresses CD19, CD20, CD10, HLA-DR, and surface immunoglobulin and may present with extranodal masses or marrow/blood involvement.

B-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma.description: B-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma is a precursor B-cell malignancy in children that commonly presents with anemia, circulating blasts, marrow disease, lymphadenopathy, or extranodal masses. However, the reported immunophenotype argues against this diagnosis.

case: A 12-year-old Malagasy boy consulted for a fever that had been evolving for two months, with a notion of trauma and pain in the right upper quadrant as well as chronic diarrhoea. A parasitological examination of the stool found eggs of Schistosoma mansoni. An ultrasound and a CT scan were then ordered.

Intestinal and hepatosplenic schistosomi.normalized_text: Intestinal and hepatosplenic schistosomiasis due to Schistosoma mansoni
Intestinal and hepatosplenic schistosomi.description: Parasitic infection caused by Schistosoma mansoni, which can produce chronic intestinal inflammation and hepatic periportal fibrosis with portal hypertension in advanced disease.

Amoebic liver abscess.description: A focal liver infection caused by Entamoeba histolytica, often presenting with prolonged fever and right upper quadrant pain; intestinal amoebiasis may cause diarrhoea.

Pyogenic liver abscess.description: A bacterial collection of pus in the liver, usually causing persistent fever, abdominal pain, and sometimes systemic illness.

Hepatic hydatid cyst.description: A liver cyst caused by Echinococcus tapeworm larvae. It may remain asymptomatic for years but can cause right upper quadrant pain, fever if infected, or symptoms after trauma-related rupture.

Traumatic liver injury with infected hem.normalized_text: Traumatic liver injury with infected hematoma or biloma
Traumatic liver injury with infected hem.description: Liver trauma can produce a hematoma or bile collection; secondary infection may lead to persistent fever and right upper quadrant pain.

case: 44-year-old man with 1 month of intermittent nonexertional substernal burning chest pain lasting hours to days, partially relieved by antacids/omeprazole, presenting with a 1-hour episode of severe pain radiating to the left arm and associated with nausea and nonbilious, nonbloody vomiting. He denied dyspnea, edema, immobility, fever, cough, or trauma. Past medical history was unremarkable, with no regular medical care for years; he denied tobacco, alcohol, and illicit drug use and had no family history of premature coronary artery disease. Exam showed marked distress but was otherwise normal: afebrile, BP 133/83 mmHg, HR 61 bpm, O2 saturation 97% on room air, no JVD, no edema, regular cardiac rhythm, clear lungs, and nontender chest and abdomen. Labs showed troponin 0.08 ng/mL, WBC 22,000/mm³ with neutrophilia and bandemia, platelets 771,000/mm³, hemoglobin 17.5 g/dL, and glucose 192 mg/dL. He reported a previously noted platelet count around 600,000/mm³ years earlier and intermittent generalized pruritus after hot showers, without bleeding, thrombosis, burning pain in hands or feet, headache, dizziness, or other neurologic symptoms.

diagnoses.name: ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction
diagnoses.icd11_title: Acute ST segment elevation myocardial infarction

Essential thrombocythemia.description: A chronic myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by persistent marked thrombocytosis and increased risk of arterial or venous thrombosis, including coronary thrombosis.

Polycythemia vera.description: A JAK2-associated myeloproliferative neoplasm with increased red-cell mass that can also cause leukocytosis and thrombocytosis; it commonly causes aquagenic pruritus and thrombotic events.

Acute coronary syndrome / non-ST-elevati.normalized_text: Acute coronary syndrome / non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction
Acute coronary syndrome / non-ST-elevati.description: Myocardial ischemia and injury due to reduced coronary blood flow, often presenting with chest pain, radiation to the arm, nausea, and elevated cardiac troponin. In this case, thrombosis related to a myeloproliferative disorder could be a potential mechanism.

Gastroesophageal reflux disease or erosi.normalized_text: Gastroesophageal reflux disease or erosive esophagitis
Gastroesophageal reflux disease or erosi.description: Reflux of gastric acid into the esophagus can cause recurrent burning substernal discomfort, often nonexertional and partially responsive to antacids or proton-pump inhibitors.

Secondary erythrocytosis and thrombocyto.normalized_text: Secondary erythrocytosis and thrombocytosis due to dehydration or physiologic stress
Secondary erythrocytosis and thrombocyto.description: Hemoconcentration from vomiting or reduced fluid intake can transiently increase hemoglobin and platelet concentrations, while acute stress or inflammation can cause leukocytosis and reactive thrombocytosis.

case: Newborn girl admitted to the NICU after cardiorespiratory arrest at delivery. Pregnancy was complicated by maternal hepatitis C infection, treated urogenital Chlamydia trachomatis infection, gestational hypertension, and prenatal right urinary tract dilatation on serial ultrasound. At 40 weeks’ gestation, after prolonged labor and cesarean delivery for nonreassuring fetal status with meconium-stained fluid, the infant was born breech with limp tone and no respiratory effort. She required 16 minutes of resuscitation, including intubation, CPR, epinephrine, and saline boluses, before spontaneous circulation returned. Apgar scores were 1, 0, 0, 1, and 3 at 1, 5, 10, 15, and 20 minutes. On NICU arrival, temperature was 34.9°C, heart rate 141 bpm, blood pressure 84/59 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation 97% on mechanical ventilation. Therapeutic hypothermia was started.

Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE) du.normalized_text: Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE) due to severe perinatal asphyxia
Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE) du.description: Brain injury caused by inadequate oxygen delivery and blood flow around the time of birth, often following prolonged fetal distress, difficult delivery, or cardiorespiratory arrest. Therapeutic hypothermia is commonly used for moderate to severe HIE.

Meconium aspiration syndrome.description: Respiratory distress caused by aspiration of meconium-contaminated amniotic fluid before or during delivery. Severe cases can cause airway obstruction, chemical pneumonitis, pulmonary hypertension, hypoxemia, and respiratory failure.

Severe neonatal depression from intrapar.normalized_text: Severe neonatal depression from intrapartum asphyxia
Severe neonatal depression from intrapar.description: Failure to establish effective breathing and circulation after birth due to oxygen deprivation during labor or delivery. It may result from placental insufficiency, umbilical cord compromise, prolonged labor, fetal distress, or complicated presentation.

case: 54-year-old man with a history of polysubstance abuse and treatment-naïve hepatitis C presented with altered mental status. He was afebrile, drowsy, and hypertensive, with distended jugular veins and bibasilar crackles. Labs showed severe renal dysfunction (creatinine 16.0 mg/dL, BUN 99 mg/dL), anemia (hemoglobin 11.3 g/dL), proteinuria with urine protein-to-creatinine ratio 1.9, elevated LDH, rare schistocytes, and low C3 with normal C4. Urine toxicology was positive for cocaine metabolites. Blood and urine cultures were negative, HIV testing was negative, and renal ultrasound showed echogenic kidneys. Family history was notable for a sister with renal failure requiring dialysis at age 45.

Cocaine-associated thrombotic microangio.description: A microvascular injury syndrome triggered by cocaine use, often associated with severe hypertension, acute kidney injury, hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and schistocytes.

Malignant hypertension causing hypertens.normalized_text: Malignant hypertension causing hypertensive nephrosclerosis and thrombotic microangiopathy
Malignant hypertension causing hypertens.description: Severe hypertension can cause acute vascular injury in the kidneys, resulting in rapidly worsening renal failure, proteinuria, hemolysis markers, and neurologic symptoms.

Hepatitis C-associated membranoprolifera.description: An immune-complex glomerulonephritis associated with chronic hepatitis C, often causing proteinuria, hematuria, reduced complement levels, hypertension, and progressive kidney dysfunction.

APOL1-associated focal segmental glomeru.normalized_text: APOL1-associated focal segmental glomerulosclerosis or chronic kidney disease
APOL1-associated focal segmental glomeru.description: APOL1-associated kidney disease is a genetic susceptibility to progressive proteinuric kidney disease, particularly in individuals of African ancestry, and can be accelerated by hypertension, infections, or substance use.

case: 44-year-old Chinese woman, previously healthy, with a 7-week history of progressively worsening nausea and vomiting with 13 kg weight loss. She denied abdominal pain, distension, or diarrhea. Initial treatment for presumed functional gastrointestinal disorder, including antidepressants, prokinetics, and anti-emetics, was ineffective. Eight days after admission, she developed metabolic alkalosis, acute respiratory failure, and neurological deficits. Examination showed right-sided limb paralysis, horizontal nystagmus, loss of pharyngeal reflex, decreased tendon reflexes on the right, and bilateral Babinski signs. Prior gastroscopy and abdominal CT were normal. Laboratory studies showed normal liver, kidney, thyroid, autoimmune, and glucose testing; serum AQP4-IgG was negative, but cerebrospinal fluid AQP4-IgG was positive.

Aquaporin-4 antibody-positive neuromyeli.normalized_text: Aquaporin-4 antibody-positive neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD) with area postrema syndrome
Aquaporin-4 antibody-positive neuromyeli.description: An autoimmune inflammatory disorder of the central nervous system associated with AQP4-IgG antibodies. Lesions involving the area postrema in the dorsal medulla can cause persistent unexplained nausea, vomiting, and hiccups; brainstem or spinal cord involvement can cause neurological deficits.

Area postrema syndrome due to NMOSD.normalized_text: Area postrema syndrome due to NMOSD
Area postrema syndrome due to NMOSD.description: Area postrema syndrome is a characteristic NMOSD presentation caused by inflammation of the vomiting center in the dorsal medulla. It produces otherwise unexplained persistent nausea, vomiting, and sometimes hiccups, often preceding more obvious neurological manifestations.

Autoimmune brainstem encephalitis/rhombe.description: Inflammation of the brainstem from autoimmune or infectious causes can produce vomiting, eye movement abnormalities, bulbar dysfunction, respiratory compromise, and upper motor neuron signs. NMOSD-related brainstem inflammation is a particularly likely autoimmune subtype in this case.

Wernicke encephalopathy secondary to pro.normalized_text: Wernicke encephalopathy secondary to prolonged vomiting and malnutrition
Wernicke encephalopathy secondary to pro.description: A neurologic emergency caused by thiamine deficiency, often after prolonged vomiting or poor intake. It classically causes ocular abnormalities, gait or coordination problems, and confusion, but presentations can be incomplete.

case: 47-year-old male with 2-month history of fever, headache, myalgia, arthralgia, and malaise. History of inguinal hernia repair surgery 10 years ago and cardiac disease. On admission, body temperature was 37.3°C. Physical examination revealed aortic valve diastolic murmurs at the precordium.

Infective endocarditis.description: Infection of the endocardial surface of the heart, most often involving a heart valve; it can cause prolonged low-grade fever, constitutional symptoms, and new or changing murmurs.

Q fever endocarditis.description: A chronic infection caused by Coxiella burnetii that can produce culture-negative endocarditis, particularly in people with pre-existing valvular or other cardiac abnormalities.

Brucella endocarditis.description: A rare but serious complication of brucellosis in which Brucella bacteria infect a heart valve, often causing prolonged fever and nonspecific musculoskeletal symptoms.

Aortic valve regurgitation.description: Leakage of blood backward through the aortic valve during diastole, producing a characteristic diastolic murmur; it may result from prior valve disease or infective endocarditis.

Systemic lupus erythematosus with Libman.normalized_text: Systemic lupus erythematosus with Libman-Sacks endocarditis
Systemic lupus erythematosus with Libman.description: An autoimmune disease that can cause fever, joint and muscle pain, constitutional symptoms, and sterile valvular vegetations known as Libman-Sacks endocarditis.

case: 51-year-old man undergoing venesection for haemochromatosis. During procedure, experienced sudden gurgling sensation up his arm, followed by severe central crushing chest pain with radiation to jaw and left arm, severe dyspnoea, and left sided hemiparesis and dysphasia. On arrival to hospital: hypoxic (oxygen saturation 88% on room air), left hemiplegia (resolved within 15 minutes). Initial ECG showed T-wave inversion inferiorly. Troponin I was raised at 0.14 μg/L (ref 0-0.08 μg/L). Transthoracic echocardiography with bubble study showed right-to-left shunting during normal respiration and Valsalva. Baseline right heart pressures were normal. Transoesophageal echocardiogram confirmed patent foramen ovale with passage of bubbles.

Paradoxical air embolism through a paten.normalized_text: Paradoxical air embolism through a patent foramen ovale
Paradoxical air embolism through a paten.description: Venous air entering during venesection can cross from the right atrium to the left atrium through a patent foramen ovale (PFO), producing systemic arterial air emboli affecting the brain and coronary circulation.

Cerebral arterial air embolism causing t.normalized_text: Cerebral arterial air embolism causing transient ischemic attack
Cerebral arterial air embolism causing t.description: Air entering the arterial circulation can obstruct cerebral vessels, causing abrupt focal neurologic deficits that may resolve rapidly if the air embolus disperses or is absorbed.

Coronary air embolism causing acute myoc.normalized_text: Coronary air embolism causing acute myocardial ischemia
Coronary air embolism causing acute myoc.description: An air embolus entering the coronary arteries can transiently obstruct coronary blood flow, leading to acute chest pain, ECG changes, and myocardial injury marker elevation.

Acute coronary syndrome due to myocardia.normalized_text: Acute coronary syndrome due to myocardial infarction
Acute coronary syndrome due to myocardia.description: Acute coronary syndrome includes myocardial ischemia or infarction, usually caused by reduced coronary blood flow. In this case, coronary air embolism would be a potential non-atherosclerotic trigger.

Patent foramen ovale.description: A patent foramen ovale is a persistent opening between the atria that can permit right-to-left shunting and allow venous emboli, including air, to bypass the lungs and enter arterial circulation.

case: 41-year-old right-handed man with neurologic history dating to his early twenties when he presented with seizures. In 2009, he developed headaches. Initial biopsy/resection pathology showed PXA (WHO grade 2) with BRAF V600E mutation confirmed by PCR testing.

Pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma (PXA), WHO.description: A rare, usually superficial astrocytic brain tumor that often affects younger patients and commonly presents with longstanding seizures. BRAF V600E mutations are frequently present.

Anaplastic pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma.description: A more aggressive variant of pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma that may arise through progression of a lower-grade PXA and can retain a BRAF V600E mutation.

Ganglioglioma.description: A usually slow-growing mixed neuronal-glial brain tumor that frequently causes chronic focal seizures in children and young adults; some cases have BRAF V600E mutations.

Dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumor (.description: A benign, epilepsy-associated glioneuronal tumor that usually develops in younger people and commonly presents with longstanding medically refractory focal seizures.

case: 32-year-old man with a 10-week history of violaceous skin rash and progressive muscle weakness. The rash began on the eyelids, elbows, metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints, and knees, followed one week later by severe generalized myalgias and worsening weakness with difficulty walking, rising from a squat, and climbing stairs. Exam at another hospital showed heliotrope rash, periungual edema, erythematous fingertip papules, and moderate-to-severe bilateral proximal muscle weakness with normal muscle bulk, tone, reflexes, and sensation. At this hospital, he had bilateral heliotrope rash, erythematous papules on the extensor surfaces of the fingers, elbows, and knees, periungual erythema, pitting edema of the arms and legs, diminished breath sounds at both lung bases, and marked generalized weakness with inability to lift arms, legs, or head against gravity. Past history included meniscal repair 10 years earlier.

Dermatomyositis.description: An idiopathic inflammatory myopathy characterized by distinctive cutaneous findings and symmetric proximal muscle weakness, often with elevated muscle enzymes and possible lung involvement.

Anti-MDA5-positive dermatomyositis.description: A dermatomyositis subtype often associated with prominent skin disease, painful palmar or fingertip papules, periungual changes, and a substantial risk of rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease; muscle weakness may be mild or severe.

Antisynthetase syndrome.description: An autoimmune inflammatory myopathy syndrome associated with myositis, interstitial lung disease, inflammatory arthritis, Raynaud phenomenon, fever, and hyperkeratotic 'mechanic's hands'; some patients have dermatomyositis-like rashes.

Polymyositis.description: An idiopathic inflammatory myopathy causing subacute symmetric proximal muscle weakness and elevated muscle enzymes, but without the characteristic cutaneous manifestations of dermatomyositis.

Immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy.description: A severe autoimmune myopathy, sometimes associated with anti-SRP or anti-HMGCR antibodies, that causes rapidly progressive symmetric proximal weakness and markedly elevated creatine kinase levels, usually with little or no skin disease.

case: A 59-year-old woman presented with a longstanding history of epilepsy with complex partial seizures, for which she had been using phenytoin for more than 20 years. She was referred with a 3-year history of progressive muscle weakness, associated with generalized bone and muscle pain, resulting in significant limitations in her daily activities. Her symptoms had further worsened with progressive proximal muscle pain and weakness and increasing bone pain. Physical examination revealed normal renal and liver function. Conventional radiographs demonstrated Looser's zones in the femoral neck bilaterally.

Phenytoin-induced osteomalacia.description: Metabolic bone disease caused by long-term phenytoin use, often through increased vitamin D breakdown, impaired calcium absorption, and secondary disturbances in bone mineralization.

Vitamin D deficiency osteomalacia.description: Defective mineralization of adult bone due to inadequate vitamin D availability, causing bone pain, muscle weakness, fractures, and pseudofractures such as Looser's zones.

Hypophosphatemic osteomalacia.description: Osteomalacia caused by chronic low phosphate levels, which impairs bone mineralization and can lead to bone pain, proximal myopathy, weakness, and insufficiency fractures.

case: A previously healthy 50-year-old man presented with acute-onset dysarthria and was found to be febrile with respiratory distress and lethargy. He performed poorly in the right hand alternating movement test. Physical examination revealed a blood pressure of 130/90 mmHg and heart rate of 116 beats per minute. The apex beat was located in the sixth intercostal space, 1.5 cm outside the midclavicular line. Cardiac auscultation revealed a grade 4/6 systolic murmur that was most prominent at the apex. Laboratory findings showed normal troponin T, creatine kinase (CK), and CK-myoglobin (CK-MB) levels, but elevated N-terminal-pro-brain natriuretic peptide (NT-pro-BNP) levels at 3277 pg/ml. The leukocyte count was 10,620/mm³ with neutrophils at 10,350/mm³, and the erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 68 mm/h. Blood culture was positive for group A β-hemolytic streptococcus. Electrocardiography revealed sinus tachycardia without evidence of ischemia.

Acute infective endocarditis with mitral.normalized_text: Acute infective endocarditis with mitral valve involvement
Acute infective endocarditis with mitral.description: A life-threatening infection of the endocardial surface of the heart, usually involving a valve. Group A beta-hemolytic streptococcus can cause acute, rapidly progressive infective endocarditis with valvular destruction, heart failure, and embolic complications.

Mitral regurgitation causing acute conge.normalized_text: Mitral regurgitation causing acute congestive heart failure
Mitral regurgitation causing acute conge.description: Mitral regurgitation occurs when the mitral valve does not close properly, allowing blood to flow backward from the left ventricle into the left atrium. Severe acute regurgitation may result from infective endocarditis and can cause pulmonary congestion and respiratory distress.

Acute ischemic stroke due to septic cere.normalized_text: Acute ischemic stroke due to septic cerebral embolism
Acute ischemic stroke due to septic cere.description: A septic embolic stroke occurs when infected material, often from an infected heart valve in infective endocarditis, travels to and obstructs a cerebral artery. It can produce sudden focal neurologic deficits.

Sepsis due to group A beta-hemolytic str.normalized_text: Sepsis due to group A beta-hemolytic streptococcal bacteremia
Sepsis due to group A beta-hemolytic str.description: Sepsis is a dysregulated systemic response to infection that can cause fever, tachycardia, respiratory distress, altered mental status, and organ dysfunction. Group A streptococcal bacteremia may cause severe invasive infection and can be associated with endocarditis.

case: Patient 1: 3.5-year-old male from unrelated Polish parents. Born at 39 weeks gestation with birth weight 3700g (50th-75th centile), length 57cm (97th centile), head circumference 36cm (75th-97th centile), thorax circumference 33cm (25-50th centile), Apgar score 9 at 1 min. Family history unremarkable. Proteinuria, hematuria and glycosuria noted in early neonatal period. UTI at 12 months. At 3 years developed bronchopneumonia with elevated creatinine. Laboratory investigations showed constant proteinuria, glycosuria, hematuria, eGFR (Schwartz) 30.56 ml/min/1.73 m2, elevated serum creatinine, uric acid, urea, total cholesterol, and triglyceride; normal CBC, blood glucose, albumin, thyroid and liver function tests. Renal ultrasound showed increased cortex echogenicity and decreased corticomedullary differentiation. Normal male karyotype (46,XY).

Dent disease (X-linked proximal tubulopa.normalized_text: Dent disease (X-linked proximal tubulopathy, usually CLCN5-related)
Dent disease (X-linked proximal tubulopa.description: An X-linked renal proximal tubular disorder characterized by low-molecular-weight proteinuria, hypercalciuria, variable glycosuria and hematuria, nephrocalcinosis or stones, and progressive chronic kidney disease.

Infantile nephropathic cystinosis.description: An autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disease caused by cystine accumulation, leading to renal Fanconi syndrome in infancy and progressive chronic kidney disease.

Renal Fanconi syndrome.description: A syndrome of generalized proximal renal tubular dysfunction causing urinary losses of glucose, proteins, phosphate, bicarbonate, uric acid, and other solutes. It may be inherited or secondary to another disorder.

Lowe syndrome (oculocerebrorenal syndrom.description: An X-linked disorder caused by OCRL gene variants, characterized by congenital cataracts, hypotonia and developmental delay, and proximal tubular dysfunction resembling Fanconi syndrome.

Congenital nephrotic syndrome.description: A severe glomerular disease presenting in the first three months of life with marked proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, edema, hyperlipidemia, and progressive renal failure. It may be genetic or secondary to congenital infection.

case: A 58-year-old man presented with a six-week history of muscle weakness, dysphagia, and a symmetrical widespread rash on the face, torso, and limbs. Laboratory testing revealed elevated creatine kinase of 7070 u/L (reference range 30-175). An oesophagogastroduodenoscopy was performed and showed abnormal findings, and a PET CT scan was arranged.

Dermatomyositis.description: An inflammatory autoimmune myopathy characterized by proximal muscle weakness, markedly elevated muscle enzymes, and characteristic symmetric skin eruptions.

Malignancy-associated dermatomyositis.description: Dermatomyositis occurring as a paraneoplastic syndrome, in which inflammatory muscle and skin disease is associated with an underlying cancer, particularly in older adults.

Polymyositis.description: An autoimmune inflammatory myopathy causing progressive symmetric proximal muscle weakness, elevated creatine kinase, and sometimes dysphagia, but without the characteristic skin findings of dermatomyositis.

Immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy.description: A severe autoimmune muscle disorder characterized by subacute proximal weakness and very high creatine kinase levels, sometimes associated with statin exposure, autoimmune disease, or malignancy.

Antisynthetase syndrome.description: A subtype of inflammatory myositis associated with autoantibodies and featuring myositis, arthritis, interstitial lung disease, Raynaud phenomenon, fever, and sometimes characteristic roughened 'mechanic's hands.'

case: An 8-year-old boy presented to his general practitioner with limping and complaints of occasional leg pain. He was otherwise healthy and afebrile. On physical examination, he walked with a limp and demonstrated painful, reduced internal rotation and abduction of his right hip. Plain radiographs were obtained to evaluate his symptoms.

Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease.description: A childhood condition caused by temporary loss of blood supply to the femoral head, leading to avascular necrosis, collapse, and remodeling of the hip joint.

Slipped capital femoral epiphysis.description: A disorder in which the femoral head slips relative to the femoral neck through the growth plate, usually occurring in adolescents and often causing hip, thigh, or knee pain.

Transient synovitis of the hip.description: A temporary inflammation of the hip joint lining, commonly occurring in children and causing acute or subacute hip pain and limp without severe systemic illness.

Septic arthritis of the hip.description: A bacterial infection within the hip joint that is a medical emergency because it can rapidly damage cartilage and bone.

Juvenile idiopathic arthritis involving.normalized_text: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis involving the hip
Juvenile idiopathic arthritis involving.description: A group of chronic inflammatory arthritis disorders beginning before age 16 that can cause joint pain, stiffness, swelling, and limitation of movement.

case: A 62-year-old fit and well Romanian man presented with a two-week history of worsening acute localized pain in the upper abdomen and vomiting. His surgical history included an open appendectomy as a child and laparoscopic cholecystectomy 20 years ago. On presentation, he had fever (39°C) and tachycardia (104 beats/min), with blood pressure of 125/73 mm Hg. Physical examination revealed generalized abdominal tenderness, worse in the right upper quadrant, with localized guarding in the right upper quadrant. Blood tests showed a raised white cell count of 16 × 10⁹/L (reference range 4-10 × 10⁹/L) and a C reactive protein concentration of 277 mg/L (reference value <9 mg/L). A frontal projection erect chest radiograph was initially reported as showing pneumoperitoneum, but showed a normal bowel gas pattern under the left hemidiaphragm.

Perforated peptic ulcer (gastric or duod.normalized_text: Perforated peptic ulcer (gastric or duodenal ulcer perforation)
Perforated peptic ulcer (gastric or duod.description: A full-thickness ulcer in the stomach or duodenum that perforates, allowing gastrointestinal contents and air to enter the peritoneal cavity, causing peritonitis and sepsis.

Contained perforated duodenal ulcer or p.normalized_text: Contained perforated duodenal ulcer or perforated duodenal diverticulum
Contained perforated duodenal ulcer or p.description: A perforation of the duodenum that becomes localized or contained by adjacent tissues, often producing right upper abdominal inflammation, retroperitoneal infection, and sepsis rather than diffuse free peritonitis.

Acute cholangitis due to retained or rec.normalized_text: Acute cholangitis due to retained or recurrent common bile duct stone
Acute cholangitis due to retained or rec.description: Infection of the biliary tree, usually caused by obstruction of the common bile duct by a stone, stricture, or malignancy. It can occur even after cholecystectomy.

Chilaiditi syndrome (colonic interpositi.description: Interposition of bowel, usually colon, between the liver and right hemidiaphragm. It can mimic free subdiaphragmatic air on chest radiography; when symptomatic it may cause abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, or bowel obstruction.

case: A 1-year and 4-month-old girl was admitted for evaluation of psychomotor retardation and an operation for exotropia. She was born at term (gestational age: 40 weeks) by cesarean delivery after an uneventful pregnancy, and was the first child of healthy, unrelated parents. The family history was unremarkable. On admission, she presented with a characteristic high-pitched cry and microcephaly. She showed delayed motor functions and crawling, was able to sit unassisted but unable to stand, with developmental characteristics lagging behind for normal chronologic age. On neurologic examination, she had left leg hypotonia, with normal tendon reflexes and normal cranial nerve signs. When she was 6 months old, ventricular septal defect was detected by echocardiography. Chromosome analysis revealed 46,XX,del (5) (p15.2) one month after delivery.

Cri-du-chat syndrome (5p deletion syndro.description: A chromosomal disorder caused by deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5, classically involving 5p15.2. It is characterized by a high-pitched cat-like cry in infancy, microcephaly, developmental delay, hypotonia, facial differences, and possible congenital heart defects.

5p15.2 deletion-associated developmental.description: A neurodevelopmental disorder resulting from deletion of genes in chromosome region 5p15.2. This region is strongly associated with the characteristic cry and severe developmental impairment seen in cri-du-chat spectrum disorders.

Global developmental delay due to a chro.normalized_text: Global developmental delay due to a chromosomal abnormality
Global developmental delay due to a chro.description: Global developmental delay describes significant delay in multiple developmental domains in young children. Chromosomal deletions are an important cause and may be accompanied by microcephaly, hypotonia, congenital anomalies, and growth or neurologic differences.

case: 7-year-old girl with no past medical history, presented with intermittent abdominal pain for about 1 month, unrelieved by anti-inflammatory treatment. Abdominal CT showed peritoneal effusion and retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy. Serum AFP was elevated to 1,210 ng/mL. Ultrasound showed multiple enlarged abdominal and retroperitoneal hypoechoic lymph nodes; the ovaries, fallopian tubes, uterus, cervix, and vagina were unremarkable. Surgical resection revealed a 4 cm jejunal mass involving the full thickness of the jejunum.

diagnoses.name: Primary yolk sac tumor of intestine
diagnoses.normalized_text: Primary yolk sac tumor of intestine
diagnoses.icd11_title: Yolk sac tumour, unspecified site, female

Primary jejunal yolk sac tumor (extragon.normalized_text: Primary jejunal yolk sac tumor (extragonadal endodermal sinus tumor)
Primary jejunal yolk sac tumor (extragon.description: A rare malignant germ-cell tumor that can arise outside the gonads, including the gastrointestinal tract. It typically produces large amounts of alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) and may spread to lymph nodes and the peritoneum.

Small intestinal lymphoma.description: A malignancy of lymphocytes that can involve the small bowel, causing bowel-wall masses, abdominal pain, mesenteric or retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy, and occasionally ascites.

Desmoplastic small round cell tumor.description: A rare aggressive sarcoma, usually arising in the abdominal or pelvic peritoneum of children and adolescents, often presenting with peritoneal masses, ascites, and lymph-node involvement.

Jejunal gastrointestinal stromal tumor (.description: A mesenchymal tumor originating from the gastrointestinal tract wall, most commonly in adults but rarely occurring in children. It may arise in the small intestine and cause abdominal pain, bleeding, or obstruction.

Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma of the gastro.normalized_text: Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma of the gastrointestinal tract
Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma of the gastro.description: A malignant childhood soft-tissue tumor derived from skeletal-muscle progenitor cells. Rarely, it can arise in the gastrointestinal tract and present as a bowel-wall mass with abdominal symptoms.

case: 6-month-old boy with 2 days of intermittent severe abdominal pain waking him from sleep, associated with crying, leg flexion, and transient abdominal rigidity. He developed three bowel movements with increasing bloody discoloration, the last nearly all blood with a large clot. History includes infantile colic and gastroesophageal reflux treated with ranitidine; recently started pureed foods and was on low-lactose cow milk-based formula. Exam showed diffuse abdominal tenderness, worse on the right, no masses or anal fissures, and later pallor with tachycardia and hypotension.

Intussusception.description: A bowel obstruction in which one segment of intestine telescopes into another, causing intermittent severe pain, intestinal ischemia, and bloody mucus stools.

Midgut volvulus due to intestinal malrot.normalized_text: Midgut volvulus due to intestinal malrotation
Midgut volvulus due to intestinal malrot.description: A congenital abnormality of intestinal rotation that can allow the bowel to twist around its blood supply, producing obstruction, ischemia, severe pain, and bloody stools.

Meckel diverticulum with bleeding.description: A congenital pouch in the small intestine that may contain acid-producing tissue, causing ulceration and painless lower gastrointestinal bleeding; it can also serve as a lead point for intussusception.

Infectious colitis or enterocolitis.description: Inflammation of the intestine caused by bacterial, viral, or other infectious organisms, which can cause abdominal pain, diarrhea, fever, and bloody stools.

Food protein-induced allergic proctocoli.normalized_text: Food protein-induced allergic proctocolitis or cow's milk protein allergy
Food protein-induced allergic proctocoli.description: An immune-mediated reaction to dietary proteins, commonly cow's milk or soy, that can cause blood-streaked stools in otherwise well young infants.

case: A 69-year-old female non-smoker presented with a 6-month history of progressive breathlessness. She had no relevant past medical history or drug history. Spirometry showed FEV1 32% predicted and a flow-volume loop suggesting severe small airway disease. Transthoracic echocardiogram was normal.

diagnoses.name: Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia
diagnoses.normalized_text: Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia
diagnoses.icd11_title: Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia

Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocr.normalized_text: Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia (DIPNECH)
Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocr.description: A rare lung disorder characterized by proliferation of pulmonary neuroendocrine cells, often causing constrictive bronchiolitis and severe airflow obstruction. It predominantly affects older non-smoking women.

Constrictive bronchiolitis (obliterative.description: A small-airway disorder in which inflammation and fibrosis narrow or obliterate bronchioles, producing fixed airflow obstruction and progressive dyspnea.

Late-onset asthma with small-airway invo.description: Asthma can present in adulthood with episodic or progressive breathlessness and obstructive spirometry caused by airway inflammation and bronchoconstriction.

Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (C.description: A chronic obstructive lung disease characterized by persistent airflow limitation, usually due to smoking or significant environmental exposures, although it may occur in non-smokers.

Bronchiectasis with obstructive small-ai.description: Bronchiectasis is permanent dilation and damage of bronchi, often associated with recurrent infection, mucus retention, cough, sputum production, and obstructive lung physiology.

case: 27-year-old man, previously healthy, presented with a few days of cough, hemoptysis, and low-grade fever. He denied night sweats and weight loss. He had a history of left supraclavicular lymph node enlargement that had fluctuated in size since age 15. On examination, he was thin, with low-grade fever, mild hypoxemia, left upper lung crackles, and a 2 cm left supraclavicular lymph node that was nontender, firm, nonfixed, circumscribed, and rubbery. Labs showed leukocytosis with neutrophilia, elevated ESR and CRP, and elevated soluble IL-2 receptor. Blood and sputum cultures were negative, autoimmune and infectious serologies were negative, and transbronchial lung biopsy showed granulomatous inflammation without identifiable pathogens.

Sarcoidosis.description: A systemic inflammatory disease characterized by noncaseating granulomas, most commonly involving the lungs and intrathoracic lymph nodes.

Tuberculosis.description: A chronic infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis that can cause pulmonary infiltrates, granulomatous inflammation, lymphadenopathy, fever, and hemoptysis.

Hodgkin lymphoma.description: A lymphoid malignancy that commonly presents in young adults with painless rubbery lymphadenopathy, often involving cervical or supraclavicular nodes, and may cause fever and elevated soluble IL-2 receptor.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis.description: An ANCA-associated vasculitis causing necrotizing granulomatous inflammation of the respiratory tract and capillaritis that can lead to cough, hemoptysis, and systemic inflammation.

Pulmonary fungal infection with granulom.normalized_text: Pulmonary fungal infection with granulomatous lymphadenitis
Pulmonary fungal infection with granulom.description: Endemic fungi such as Histoplasma, Coccidioides, or Cryptococcus can produce pulmonary granulomas, cough, fever, hemoptysis, and regional or mediastinal lymphadenopathy.

case: A 31-year-old Caucasian man with multiple sclerosis who had received 24 natalizumab infusions and was switched to fingolimod due to persistent high anti-JCPyV antibody index (3.61).
