After 40 days of fingolimod treatment, he developed seizures and visual field defects. Neurological examination revealed lateral nystagmus to the left, homonymous hemianopia, distal tremor and spasm of the upper limbs. He presented with leukopenia (0.83 × 10^9/L) at hospital admission.

Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopat.normalized_text: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) due to JC polyomavirus reactivation
Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopat.description: A severe opportunistic demyelinating brain infection caused by JC polyomavirus, most often occurring in immunosuppressed patients, including those previously treated with natalizumab.

Multiple sclerosis relapse.description: An acute or subacute episode of new inflammatory demyelination in the central nervous system causing new neurological deficits lasting more than 24 hours.

Fingolimod-associated lymphopenia with o.normalized_text: Fingolimod-associated lymphopenia with opportunistic central nervous system infection
Fingolimod-associated lymphopenia with o.description: Fingolimod can cause substantial peripheral lymphocyte sequestration and leukopenia, increasing susceptibility to opportunistic infections such as PML, varicella-zoster encephalitis, cryptococcal infection, or other viral encephalitides.

Posterior reversible encephalopathy synd.description: A neurotoxic syndrome characterized by vasogenic edema, usually involving posterior brain regions, that can cause seizures and visual disturbances; it is often associated with hypertension, renal dysfunction, immunosuppressive therapy, or endothelial injury.

case: A 39-year-old Korean male presented with intermittent and atypical chest discomfort symptoms. His medical history included burning pain originating in the extremities and radiating inwards to the limbs since childhood, which was previously dismissed as 'growing pains'. He also experienced ringing in the ears, had angiokeratomas on his trunk, and cornea verticillata. Physical examination revealed proteinuria (P/C ratio 0.501) without hematuria and normal renal function. His plasma αGal-A activity was markedly lower than controls at 4.1 nmoL/hr/mg protein (normal cutoff >35 nmoL/hr/mg protein). Genetic testing identified a hemizygous mutation in exon 4 of GLA, c.617T>C (p.Leu206 Pro).

Fabry disease (classic X-linked lysosoma.normalized_text: Fabry disease (classic X-linked lysosomal storage disorder due to GLA mutation)
Fabry disease (classic X-linked lysosoma.description: A rare X-linked lysosomal storage disease caused by deficient alpha-galactosidase A activity, leading to globotriaosylceramide accumulation in vascular, renal, cardiac, neurologic, skin, and ocular tissues.

Fabry-associated cardiomyopathy / cardia.normalized_text: Fabry-associated cardiomyopathy / cardiac involvement of Fabry disease
Fabry-associated cardiomyopathy / cardia.description: Cardiac Fabry disease results from glycosphingolipid deposition in cardiomyocytes and coronary microvasculature, potentially causing chest pain, left ventricular hypertrophy, arrhythmias, conduction abnormalities, and heart failure.

Fabry nephropathy.description: Renal involvement in Fabry disease caused by glycosphingolipid accumulation in podocytes, tubular cells, vascular cells, and glomerular cells. It commonly presents with proteinuria and may progress to chronic kidney disease.

Small-fiber neuropathy secondary to Fabr.normalized_text: Small-fiber neuropathy secondary to Fabry disease
Small-fiber neuropathy secondary to Fabr.description: Fabry disease frequently causes small-fiber peripheral neuropathy due to glycosphingolipid deposition and dysfunction of sensory and autonomic nerve fibers, producing burning pain and pain crises beginning in childhood.

case: A multitrauma patient was admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) due to an intrahepatic hematoma. On the 7th day of ICU hospitalization, he presented fever. Laboratory blood tests showed leucocytosis and elevated liver function values.

Infected intrahepatic hematoma.description: A traumatic liver hematoma can become secondarily infected during prolonged ICU hospitalization, causing localized hepatic infection and systemic inflammatory signs.

Pyogenic liver abscess.description: A pyogenic liver abscess is a collection of pus within the liver, potentially developing from infection of a traumatic hepatic hematoma, biliary infection, or bloodstream infection.

Acute cholangitis.description: Acute cholangitis is infection of the biliary tract, usually caused by biliary obstruction, and may produce fever, inflammatory laboratory abnormalities, and abnormal liver tests.

Acute acalculous cholecystitis.description: Acute acalculous cholecystitis is gallbladder inflammation without gallstones, often occurring in critically ill trauma or ICU patients.

Drug-induced liver injury with concurren.normalized_text: Drug-induced liver injury with concurrent inflammatory response
Drug-induced liver injury with concurren.description: Medications commonly used in ICU patients, including antibiotics, analgesics, anticonvulsants, and sedatives, can cause liver enzyme elevations; some drug reactions can also cause fever and leukocytosis.

case: A 57-year-old man presented to the emergency department with a 12-hour history of hematuria. Several hours after intravenous urography was performed with iodinated contrast material, generalized pustular eruptions developed, with multiple coalescing vesicles and pus-filled bullae observed on the trunk, arms, and legs. Laboratory studies revealed neutrophilia and mild eosinophilia with 55% neutrophils and 8% eosinophils, and a white-cell count of 6500 per cubic millimeter. Histopathological examination of the lesions showed pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia, full-thickness epidermal necrosis, and a diffuse neutrophilic dermal infiltrate. Microbiologic studies were negative.

Acute generalized exanthematous pustulos.normalized_text: Acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP) induced by iodinated contrast media
Acute generalized exanthematous pustulos.description: A severe acute drug-related pustular eruption, commonly triggered by medications including iodinated contrast agents, characterized by sudden widespread sterile pustules, neutrophilic inflammation, and sometimes vesicles or bullae.

Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal.normalized_text: Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis (SJS/TEN) spectrum due to iodinated contrast
Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal.description: A rare, severe immune-mediated drug reaction causing widespread keratinocyte death, epidermal detachment, bullae, and mucosal erosions; toxic epidermal necrolysis represents the more extensive form.

Generalized bullous fixed drug eruption.normalized_text: Generalized bullous fixed drug eruption caused by iodinated contrast media
Generalized bullous fixed drug eruption.description: A drug-induced hypersensitivity reaction in which sharply demarcated erythematous or violaceous lesions recur after exposure and may become widespread with blisters and epidermal necrosis in generalized bullous forms.

Generalized pustular psoriasis.description: A severe inflammatory psoriasis variant characterized by abrupt widespread sterile pustules, often accompanied by systemic inflammation and neutrophilia; it may be triggered by medications, infection, or withdrawal of corticosteroids.

case: 54-year-old female with hypertension and hyperlipidemia presented to cardiology clinic for follow-up 20 months since her most recent office visit. She was being evaluated for follow-up of cardiac risk factors and medication management. The patient was in her usual state of health and asymptomatic without changes in her exercise tolerance, weight, or energy levels. She did not have any gross hematuria or flank pain.

45-year-old man presented with acute nausea, epigastric pain, and vomiting սկսing the day before admission. He had been bitten on the hands and forearms by his dog 3 days earlier, with additional recent head trauma from a rusty nail and dental extractions 1–2 weeks prior. Past history included asthma, mild COPD, anxiety, depression, chronic back pain, and heavy alcohol use, with recent intake up to 18 beers daily, stopped 3 days before admission. On examination, he was ill-appearing, anxious, and diaphoretic, with temperature 35.6°C, blood pressure 154/102 mmHg, pulse 110 bpm, respiratory rate 28/min, and oxygen saturation 100% on room air. He had numerous lacerations with necrotic edges and scratches on both hands and forearms, including a 3–4 cm right forearm lesion with a 5–7 cm purplish surrounding border, and capillary refill of 5 seconds.

Capnocytophaga canimorsus infection with.description: A potentially fulminant bloodstream infection caused by bacteria transmitted through dog bites or saliva. Risk is increased by heavy alcohol use and can cause shock, purpuric skin lesions, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and tissue necrosis.

Necrotizing soft-tissue infection.description: A rapidly progressive bacterial infection involving the deep skin, fascia, or muscle that can follow traumatic wounds or animal bites and may cause necrosis, systemic toxicity, and sepsis.

Alcohol withdrawal syndrome.description: A syndrome occurring after abrupt reduction or cessation of heavy alcohol consumption, producing autonomic hyperactivity, anxiety, tremor, nausea, vomiting, and potentially seizures or delirium tremens.

Tetanus.description: A toxin-mediated neurologic disease caused by Clostridium tetani entering contaminated wounds, including puncture wounds from rusty objects or animal bites. It typically causes muscle rigidity, painful spasms, and autonomic instability.

Acute pancreatitis, possibly alcohol-rel.description: Inflammation of the pancreas, commonly caused by heavy alcohol use, which typically presents with acute epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting.

case: 27-year-old female, 162cm tall, 30kg weight. Born after normal pregnancy/delivery. No family history of neurological diseases. Normal early development. At age 6, developed general muscle weakness and gait disturbance with decreased muscle tone/strength and atrophic muscle mass. At age 8, muscle biopsy showed mitochondrial myopathy of pleoconial type. At age 24, had sudden syncope. At age 26, had stroke with general weakness, aphagia, and dysarthria. Current presentation at age 27 with left hemiplegia and aphasia. Lab findings: plasma lactate 21.8 mg/dL (elevated), normal CBC/electrolytes/BUN/creatinine, free T4 1.76 ng/dL, TSH 0.04 μIU/mL, C3 13 mg/dL (low), C4 18 mg/dL (normal). Negative for ASO antibody, rheumatoid factor, anti-dsDNA, lupus anticoagulants, and anti-cytoplasmic antibody. DNA sequencing showed m.3303C>T mutation in mitochondrial tRNA leucine 1 gene.

diagnoses.name: MELAS syndrome
diagnoses.icd11_title: MELAS - [Mitochondrial encephalopathy with lactic acidosis and stroke-like episodes] syndrome

MELAS syndrome (mitochondrial encephalom.normalized_text: MELAS syndrome (mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and stroke-like episodes)
MELAS syndrome (mitochondrial encephalom.description: A mitochondrial disorder, commonly caused by mutations in mitochondrial tRNA genes, characterized by progressive muscle disease, lactic acidosis, neurologic dysfunction, and recurrent stroke-like episodes before age 40. The m.3303C>T mutation in the mitochondrial tRNA leucine 1 gene is consistent with a MELAS-spectrum disorder.

Mitochondrial myopathy due to MT-TL1 mut.normalized_text: Mitochondrial myopathy due to MT-TL1 mutation
Mitochondrial myopathy due to MT-TL1 mut.description: A group of mitochondrial muscle disorders caused by impaired oxidative phosphorylation, often due to mutations in the mitochondrial tRNA leucine 1 gene. These disorders can cause progressive weakness, muscle wasting, exercise intolerance, lactic acidosis, and variable neurologic complications.

Mitochondrial stroke-like episode second.normalized_text: Mitochondrial stroke-like episode secondary to MELAS-spectrum disease
Mitochondrial stroke-like episode second.description: A stroke-like episode is an acute focal neurologic event caused by mitochondrial energy failure rather than a conventional arterial blockage. It commonly causes transient or persistent weakness, language impairment, seizures, visual symptoms, and altered consciousness in patients with MELAS-spectrum mitochondrial disease.

Maternally inherited diabetes and deafne.normalized_text: Maternally inherited diabetes and deafness (MIDD), MT-TL1-related mitochondrial disease
Maternally inherited diabetes and deafne.description: MIDD is an MT-TL1-associated mitochondrial disorder usually characterized by diabetes mellitus and sensorineural hearing loss, sometimes with myopathy, cardiomyopathy, and neurologic manifestations. It can overlap genetically and clinically with MELAS.

case: 29-year-old woman with a 7-week history of progressive generalized pruritus, nausea, bloating, and watery mustard-colored diarrhea დაწყ after eating sushi. Three weeks into illness, she developed jaundice, right upper quadrant discomfort, decreased appetite, and dark amber urine. Prior labs showed elevated ALT 327 U/L, AST 104 U/L, total bilirubin 5.8 mg/dL, and CA 19-9 73 U/mL. Past history of anxiety and depression; no medications or drug allergies. On examination, she was thin, jaundiced with scleral icterus, and had diffuse excoriations from scratching.

Acute hepatitis A.description: A fecal-oral viral hepatitis that can be acquired from contaminated food, including raw or undercooked seafood, causing an acute hepatocellular illness with jaundice.

Acute hepatitis E.description: A foodborne viral hepatitis that may be associated with undercooked pork, game, or shellfish and can produce acute hepatitis with cholestatic jaundice and pruritus.

Choledocholithiasis with obstructive jau.description: A gallstone lodged in the common bile duct can obstruct bile flow, causing conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, dark urine, itching, jaundice, and right upper quadrant discomfort.

Primary sclerosing cholangitis.description: A chronic inflammatory disease causing multifocal narrowing of the intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts, leading to cholestasis, itching, jaundice, and increased risk of cholangiocarcinoma.

Cholangiocarcinoma.description: Cancer of the bile ducts that can cause biliary obstruction, progressive itching, painless or mildly painful jaundice, dark urine, weight loss, and elevated CA 19-9.

case: A patient with known Crohn's disease presented with difficulties to pass stool, a sensation of a foreign body in the rectum and limited rectal bleeding. An endoscopy was performed as the first examination. A gallstone was found in the rectum and it was removed without complications.

Rectal gallstone impaction (distal galls.description: A rare form of gallstone ileus in which a gallstone enters the gastrointestinal tract, usually through a biliary-enteric fistula, migrates distally, and becomes lodged in the rectum.

Gallstone ileus due to a cholecystoenter.normalized_text: Gallstone ileus due to a cholecystoenteric fistula
Gallstone ileus due to a cholecystoenter.description: Mechanical intestinal obstruction caused by a gallstone entering the bowel through an abnormal connection between the gallbladder and intestine; obstruction is usually in the small bowel but can rarely occur in the colon or rectum.

Crohn's disease with anorectal or coloni.normalized_text: Crohn's disease with anorectal or colonic stricture
Crohn's disease with anorectal or coloni.description: Crohn's disease can cause chronic inflammation and scarring that narrows the rectum, anus, or colon, leading to obstructive defecatory symptoms.

Fecal impaction.description: Accumulation of hardened stool in the rectum that can cause obstructed defecation, rectal pressure, and minor mucosal bleeding.

Rectal neoplasm.description: A benign or malignant rectal mass can produce altered bowel evacuation, rectal fullness, bleeding, and symptoms of partial obstruction.

case: 15-year-old boy presented after injuring his left knee while carrying a tray of food at a fast food restaurant. He felt his knee 'wobble' and fell to the floor, unable to bear weight due to pain. Medical history included chronic fatigue syndrome. Had a Beighton score of 6 (indicating joint laxity) but no history of joint dislocations. On examination: laterally dislocated patella, moderate effusion, pain on palpation around medial patellofemoral ligament, range of movement reduced to extension-flexion of 0/10/60 degrees, ligamentous tests unremarkable. Two weeks later: complained of intermittent locking in left knee, had joint effusion and palpable loose body under patella.

Acute lateral patellar dislocation.description: Displacement of the patella toward the outer side of the knee, often occurring after twisting or minor trauma in patients with patellar instability or generalized joint laxity.

Osteochondral fracture with intra-articu.normalized_text: Osteochondral fracture with intra-articular loose body after patellar dislocation
Osteochondral fracture with intra-articu.description: A fracture or shearing injury of cartilage and underlying bone, commonly from the patella or lateral femoral condyle after patellar dislocation, which can create a loose fragment inside the joint.

Recurrent patellofemoral instability due.normalized_text: Recurrent patellofemoral instability due to generalized joint hypermobility
Recurrent patellofemoral instability due.description: A tendency for the patella to partially or fully dislocate because of lax supporting tissues, abnormal patellar tracking, or generalized hypermobility.

Meniscal tear.description: A tear of the medial or lateral meniscus, the shock-absorbing cartilage in the knee, which may cause pain, swelling, mechanical locking, and difficulty bearing weight after injury.

case: 45-year-old female with 13-year history of papular spiny eruptions on trunk and limbs with severe pruritus. Patient was otherwise in good health. Family history positive for psoriasis in sister. Treatment history included topical steroids and oral antihistamines without relief. Papular lesions on body presented before the alopecia of scalp and pubis, while axillae had been involved for 6 years.

Graham-Little-Piccardi-Lassueur syndrome.description: A rare variant of lichen planopilaris characterized by follicular keratotic or spiny papules on the body, scarring alopecia of the scalp, and non-scarring hair loss in axillary and pubic regions.

Lichen planopilaris.description: An inflammatory follicular form of lichen planus that causes perifollicular inflammation, itching, and usually permanent scarring hair loss of the scalp; it may be associated with follicular papules elsewhere on the body.

Lichen spinulosus.description: A follicular keratotic disorder producing groups of rough, spiny papules, commonly on the trunk and extremities, sometimes with itching.

Keratosis pilaris.description: A common benign follicular keratinization disorder causing small rough papules, often on the arms, thighs, trunk, or buttocks; it is usually mild and may occasionally itch.

Follicular mucinosis.description: An inflammatory condition in which mucin accumulates in hair follicles, causing follicular papules or plaques and sometimes localized hair loss; persistent adult cases may require evaluation for associated cutaneous lymphoma.

case: 35-year-old woman with a history of preeclampsia in a pregnancy 12 months earlier, delivered by Caesarean at 29 weeks, followed by poorly controlled hypertension and proteinuria >1 g/day. Over the preceding 6 months, she developed fatigue, headaches, severe hypertension, and facial and pedal edema. On admission she had severe hypertension, pallor, edema, renal failure, anemia, and thrombocytopenia. Examination showed blood pressure 151/103 mmHg. Laboratory findings included hemoglobin 7.5 g/dL, platelets 46 × 10⁹/L, urea 182 mg/dL, creatinine 6.46 mg/dL, proteinuria 4.9 g/24 h, hematuria, elevated LDH and bilirubin, low haptoglobin, increased reticulocytes, schistocytes, and negative Coombs test. Liver enzymes, immunologic tests, viral screening, and antiphospholipid antibodies were normal.

Complement-mediated atypical hemolytic u.description: A thrombotic microangiopathy caused by dysregulated complement activation, often triggered by pregnancy or the postpartum period, leading to microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, severe kidney injury, and hypertension.

Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP.description: A life-threatening thrombotic microangiopathy, usually due to severe ADAMTS13 deficiency, characterized by thrombocytopenia and microangiopathic hemolytic anemia; neurologic symptoms, fever, and renal dysfunction may occur.

Malignant hypertension-associated thromb.description: Severely elevated blood pressure can damage renal arterioles and cause a thrombotic microangiopathy with hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, progressive kidney failure, hematuria, and proteinuria.

Preeclampsia-related thrombotic microang.normalized_text: Preeclampsia-related thrombotic microangiopathy or persistent postpartum preeclampsia-associated renal injury
Preeclampsia-related thrombotic microang.description: Preeclampsia is a pregnancy-specific hypertensive disorder characterized by hypertension and proteinuria, sometimes complicated by hemolysis, thrombocytopenia, and renal injury; these abnormalities generally improve after delivery.

case: 45-year-old woman presented with syncope and severe anemia (hemoglobin 6 g/dL) with lower GI bleeding. A diagnostic colonoscopy was negative. CT scan of abdomen and pelvis revealed a 3.2 x 3 x 2.9 cm contrast-enhancing right lower-quadrant mass arising from the wall of the ileum. No evidence of metastatic disease. Subsequent laparotomy found a 3.5 cm mass that was resected with negative margins. Molecular studies showed a 42-base pair deletion in exon 11 of the KIT gene (V559_D572del) that would delete all or part of codons 558 to 572 and would change the 558-encoding amino acid from Lys to Asn (K558N).

diagnoses.name: Gastrointestinal stromal tumor
diagnoses.icd11_title: Gastrointestinal stromal tumour of unspecified gastrointestinal sites

Ileal gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GI.description: A mesenchymal tumor of the gastrointestinal tract arising from interstitial cells of Cajal. Small-bowel GISTs commonly harbor activating KIT mutations, particularly in exon 11, and may present with gastrointestinal bleeding from mucosal ulceration.

Small-bowel adenocarcinoma.description: A malignant epithelial tumor of the small intestine that can cause occult or overt gastrointestinal bleeding, anemia, abdominal pain, or obstruction. It is not typically associated with KIT exon 11 activating mutations.

Ileal neuroendocrine tumor (small-bowel.description: A slow-growing neuroendocrine neoplasm that often arises in the distal ileum. It may present as a small enhancing bowel-wall mass and can cause bleeding or obstruction, although carcinoid syndrome usually occurs only with metastatic disease.

Small-bowel lymphoma.description: A lymphoid malignancy involving the small intestine that may produce bowel-wall thickening, a mass, bleeding, anemia, abdominal pain, weight loss, or obstructive symptoms.

Meckel diverticulum with ectopic gastric.normalized_text: Meckel diverticulum with ectopic gastric mucosa
Meckel diverticulum with ectopic gastric.description: A congenital ileal diverticulum that can ulcerate adjacent mucosa because of acid secretion from ectopic gastric tissue, causing painless lower gastrointestinal bleeding and iron-deficiency anemia. It usually does not form a solid enhancing ileal-wall tumor.

case: A 73-year-old man presented with abdominal distention and maldigestion for 1 month. The patient had a medical history of diabetes and hypertension. On physical examination, an intraabdominal mass was palpated in the epigastric area, and the patient did not complain of pain and tenderness. Laboratory findings showed no abnormalities except an elevated fasting glucose level.

diagnoses.name: Malignant gastrointestinal stromal tumor
diagnoses.icd11_title: Malignant GIST - [gastrointestinal stromal tumour] of large intestine

Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.description: A malignant tumor arising from the pancreatic ducts, often presenting in older adults with weight loss, abdominal discomfort, jaundice, or impaired digestion due to pancreatic obstruction.

Pancreatic cystic neoplasm (such as muci.normalized_text: Pancreatic cystic neoplasm (such as mucinous cystic neoplasm or intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm)
Pancreatic cystic neoplasm (such as muci.description: A fluid-containing pancreatic tumor that may become large and cause abdominal fullness, palpable mass, or digestive symptoms; some types can progress to pancreatic cancer.

Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor.description: A tumor arising from hormone-producing pancreatic cells. Nonfunctioning tumors may grow silently and present with a palpable mass, abdominal fullness, or digestive symptoms.

Gastrointestinal stromal tumor of the st.normalized_text: Gastrointestinal stromal tumor of the stomach
Gastrointestinal stromal tumor of the st.description: A mesenchymal tumor of the gastrointestinal tract, most commonly arising in the stomach. Larger tumors can present as a painless upper abdominal mass or abdominal fullness.

Pancreatic pseudocyst.description: A collection of pancreatic fluid surrounded by a fibrous wall, usually developing after acute or chronic pancreatitis. Large pseudocysts may cause abdominal distention and digestive compression symptoms.

case: A 58-year-old overweight African American male presented with a 5-year history of a slightly pruritic and painful rash that worsened during summers, and blisters sometimes developed. Emollients were unhelpful. The patient was otherwise healthy, performed indoor manual labor as a maintenance engineer, and had no significant sun exposure. His sister had diabetes mellitus and a similar rash in her axillae. Physical examination revealed irregularly thickened skin containing hyperpigmentation, hypopigmentation, multiple acrochordons (skin tags), malodorous crust, and areas of maceration and erosion. Further examination showed pseudofolliculitis barbae in the submental and mandibular regions bilaterally. The nails, oral cavity, and mucosal membranes appeared normal.

Hailey-Hailey disease (familial benign c.description: A rare inherited acantholytic skin disorder causing recurrent painful, pruritic erosions, fissures, crusting, and occasional blisters in flexural areas, often worsened by heat, sweating, and friction.

Darier disease (keratosis follicularis).description: An inherited disorder of keratinization characterized by greasy, crusted keratotic papules in seborrheic or flexural areas, often exacerbated by heat, sweating, and sun exposure.

Intertrigo with secondary bacterial or f.normalized_text: Intertrigo with secondary bacterial or fungal infection
Intertrigo with secondary bacterial or f.description: Inflammation of opposing skin surfaces due to moisture, friction, and heat, frequently complicated by Candida, bacteria, or mixed microbial overgrowth causing odor, maceration, crusting, and erosions.

case: A 22-year-old female presented with a gradually increasing pelvic mass with tenderness for 1 month. There was no evidence of previous trauma or fever, and no history of other medical or surgical disease and no evidence of pregnancy. On physical examination, there was a palpable mass with tenderness in her left pelvic area.

Ovarian cyst (functional or hemorrhagic.description: A fluid-filled sac arising from the ovary; functional cysts are common in reproductive-age women and may enlarge or bleed, causing pelvic pain or tenderness.

Ovarian neoplasm (benign ovarian tumor s.normalized_text: Ovarian neoplasm (benign ovarian tumor such as cystadenoma or dermoid cyst)
Ovarian neoplasm (benign ovarian tumor s.description: A benign or malignant growth arising from the ovary that can present as an enlarging pelvic or abdominal mass; benign tumors are more common in young women.

Endometrioma.description: An ovarian cyst caused by endometriosis, containing old blood and often associated with chronic pelvic pain, menstrual pain, and tenderness.

Ovarian torsion due to an adnexal mass.normalized_text: Ovarian torsion due to an adnexal mass
Ovarian torsion due to an adnexal mass.description: Twisting of the ovary, often around an ovarian cyst or tumor, which compromises blood supply and usually causes pelvic pain and adnexal tenderness.

Pelvic inflammatory disease with tubo-ov.normalized_text: Pelvic inflammatory disease with tubo-ovarian abscess
Pelvic inflammatory disease with tubo-ov.description: An upper genital tract infection that may form an inflammatory mass involving the fallopian tube and ovary, often causing pelvic pain, tenderness, and fever.

case: 36-year-old female with no past medical history who developed lower limbs and para-spinal muscle spasms that progressed over 3 months. Her symptoms continued to progress and she became wheelchair-bound 6 months later. When reviewed at institution, she was severely disabled requiring regular IVIG treatments at a dose of 90g every 12 days. She was taking regular diazepam at a dose of 30mg per day and morphine up to 60mg a day to control pain. On examination, she had brisk reflexes and severe clonus. The muscle spasms were severe enough to compromise her breathing and she required intermittent oxygen.

Stiff-person syndrome (SPS).description: A rare autoimmune neurologic disorder characterized by progressive axial and limb muscle stiffness, painful spasms, exaggerated reflexes, and stimulus-sensitive episodes. It is often associated with anti-GAD antibodies and may respond to benzodiazepines and IVIG.

Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigid.normalized_text: Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus (PERM)
Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigid.description: A severe autoimmune disorder within the stiff-person spectrum, often associated with glycine receptor antibodies. It causes marked rigidity, stimulus-sensitive spasms, hyperreflexia, myoclonus, brainstem dysfunction, autonomic symptoms, and potentially respiratory failure.

Hereditary spastic paraplegia.description: A group of genetic neurodegenerative disorders causing progressive upper motor neuron dysfunction, predominantly affecting the lower limbs and leading to spasticity, hyperreflexia, clonus, and gait impairment.

Primary lateral sclerosis.description: A slowly progressive motor neuron disorder involving upper motor neurons, causing spasticity, hyperreflexia, clonus, stiffness, and progressive weakness without prominent lower motor neuron findings early in the disease.

Tetanus.description: An acute toxin-mediated neurologic illness caused by Clostridium tetani, producing painful generalized rigidity, spasms, hyperreflexia, and potentially life-threatening respiratory muscle involvement.

case: 46-year-old woman presented with frequent collapse. Medical history included carotid endarterectomy in 2005 following a small right hemispheric stroke, and hypercholesterolaemia. No previous dermatological or scalp problems. Current medications: clopidogrel 75mg, aspirin 80mg, and simvastatin 40mg daily.

Cardiac arrhythmia (for example, bradyar.normalized_text: Cardiac arrhythmia (for example, bradyarrhythmia or tachyarrhythmia)
Cardiac arrhythmia (for example, bradyar.description: An abnormal heart rhythm can transiently reduce cerebral blood flow and cause recurrent collapse or syncope.

Orthostatic hypotension.description: A fall in blood pressure on standing can cause dizziness, fainting, or collapse because of reduced blood flow to the brain.

Transient ischaemic attack or recurrent.normalized_text: Transient ischaemic attack or recurrent cerebrovascular insufficiency
Transient ischaemic attack or recurrent.description: Temporary reduction or interruption of cerebral blood flow may produce transient neurological symptoms and can occasionally present with falls or collapse, particularly in a patient with established vascular disease.

case: 60-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis on methotrexate and adalimumab, admitted after a burn from an electric heater. Four months earlier she developed pain and stiffness in the MCP and interphalangeal joints, right ankle, and both knees. Six weeks before admission she had severe arthralgia, low-grade fever, livedo reticularis on the legs, and purpuric lesions around the malleoli. Labs then showed anemia, leukopenia/neutropenia, elevated rheumatoid factor, hypergammaglobulinemia, positive ANA, low C4, mildly positive anti-dsDNA, and positive cryoglobulins; HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C tests were negative. On admission she had fever and pancytopenia, without hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy; blood film, cultures, chest/abdomen/pelvis CT, CMV PCR, and tuberculin test were negative. She had traveled to Athens 7 months earlier and stayed with relatives who kept several dogs.

Visceral leishmaniasis.description: A systemic protozoal infection caused by Leishmania species, transmitted by sandflies and associated with exposure to infected dogs in Mediterranean regions. It can cause fever, pancytopenia, hypergammaglobulinemia, autoimmune serologies, and vasculitic manifestations, particularly in immunosuppressed patients.

Systemic lupus erythematosus.description: A systemic autoimmune connective-tissue disease that may cause inflammatory arthritis, cytopenias, low complement levels, positive ANA and anti-dsDNA antibodies, fever, and cutaneous vasculitic lesions.

Mixed cryoglobulinemic vasculitis.description: An immune-complex small-vessel vasculitis caused by circulating cryoglobulins. It commonly produces palpable purpura, livedo, arthralgia, low complement levels, elevated rheumatoid factor, and constitutional symptoms; it may be associated with hepatitis C, autoimmune disease, lymphoproliferative disease, or infections.

Felty syndrome.description: A complication of longstanding seropositive rheumatoid arthritis characterized classically by neutropenia and splenomegaly, often with recurrent infections and high rheumatoid factor levels.

Methotrexate-associated lymphoproliferat.description: An immunosuppression-associated lymphoid proliferation or lymphoma occurring in patients receiving methotrexate, often in rheumatoid arthritis. It can present with fever, cytopenias, constitutional symptoms, lymphadenopathy, extranodal disease, or bone marrow involvement.

case: A 25-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus presented to the emergency department for evaluation of a hyperpigmented lesion on the shin. The lesion appeared as a small reddish-brown macule 3 years ago and has gradually increased in size. During the past several months, the lesion has become indented and increasingly tender. The patient denies systemic symptoms, including fevers and chills, and is primarily concerned about the changing appearance of the lesion and the new-onset tenderness. Laboratory evaluation shows a random blood glucose level of 217 mg/dL (12 mmol/L).

Necrobiosis lipoidica.description: A chronic granulomatous skin disorder strongly associated with diabetes mellitus, typically causing slowly enlarging yellow-brown or reddish-brown plaques on the shins with central atrophy or indentation.

Diabetic dermopathy.description: A common diabetes-associated skin finding consisting of small, round or oval brown macules or mildly atrophic patches, most often on the anterior shins.

Dermatofibroma.description: A benign fibrous skin tumor that commonly appears as a slowly growing brown, red-brown, or hyperpigmented papule or nodule on the lower extremities and may show dimpling when compressed.

Cutaneous melanoma.description: A malignant tumor of melanocytes that can present as a changing pigmented lesion with progressive enlargement, color variation, surface change, pain, or tenderness.

case: 14-year-old boy with 2 days of acute fear of choking while swallowing after choking on chicken at dinner, followed by vomiting with attempted eating, marked reduction in oral intake, and drooling; on the day of presentation he took only small sips of water and slept most of the day. Mother also reported inspiratory stridor during sleep over the preceding few weeks. Past history includes infantile gastroesophageal reflux, milk-protein allergy, sensory-integration training in childhood, keratosis pilaris, eczema, incomplete immunizations after age 2.5 years, and no current medications. Examination showed an alert, anxious-appearing boy with persistent involuntary burping, dry oral mucosa, and drooling; vital signs were stable. Neurologic exam was normal, but later exam noted hypertonic leg muscles and mildly positive left Chvostek's sign.

Specific phobia of choking (phagophobia).normalized_text: Specific phobia of choking (phagophobia) with avoidant/restrictive food intake
Specific phobia of choking (phagophobia).description: An anxiety-related fear of swallowing or choking that can begin abruptly after a frightening choking event and lead to avoidance of food and liquids.

Esophageal food bolus impaction or retai.normalized_text: Esophageal food bolus impaction or retained esophageal foreign body
Esophageal food bolus impaction or retai.description: A piece of food or another material lodged in the esophagus can cause acute dysphagia, drooling, gagging, vomiting, and inability to tolerate normal oral intake.

Eosinophilic esophagitis.description: A chronic allergic inflammatory disorder of the esophagus, often associated with eczema, food allergy, or other atopic conditions, that may cause dysphagia and food impaction.

Gastroesophageal reflux disease with eso.description: Reflux of stomach contents into the esophagus can cause inflammation, nausea, vomiting, swallowing discomfort, and feeding avoidance; severe esophagitis can contribute to dysphagia.

Hypocalcemia, potentially related to poo.normalized_text: Hypocalcemia, potentially related to poor intake or an underlying metabolic disorder
Hypocalcemia, potentially related to poo.description: Low blood calcium can cause neuromuscular irritability, including muscle stiffness, tetany, paresthesias, and positive Chvostek's sign. It may worsen with reduced oral intake or vomiting.

case: 57-year-old woman with resected stage IIIC cutaneous melanoma presented with recurrent fever. Four months earlier, she developed bleeding from a right scalp lesion; evaluation showed ulcerated melanoma with positive margins. Three months earlier, she underwent wide local excision and neck lymph-node dissection, which showed metastatic melanoma in 2 of 26 nodes; BRAF V600E mutation was identified. One month before admission, she started adjuvant dabrafenib and trametinib, and fever with nausea began the next day, resolving after temporary discontinuation and antipyretics. Fever recurred two weeks before admission. On presentation, temperature was 40.2°C, blood pressure 85/53 mm Hg, pulse 108 bpm, oxygen saturation 94% on room air; she was diaphoretic, ill-appearing, with mild right upper quadrant tenderness and no rash.

Dabrafenib and trametinib-associated dru.description: A common adverse effect of BRAF and MEK inhibitor therapy, particularly dabrafenib plus trametinib, causing recurrent high fever that may be accompanied by chills, nausea, dehydration, hypotension, and flu-like symptoms.

Sepsis.description: A life-threatening systemic inflammatory response to infection that can cause fever, tachycardia, hypotension, diaphoresis, and toxic appearance; patients receiving cancer therapy may be at increased risk of infection.

Acute cholangitis.description: A bacterial infection of the biliary tract, usually due to biliary obstruction, classically causing fever, right upper quadrant abdominal pain, and jaundice; severe cases can cause hypotension and sepsis.

Tumor fever due to melanoma.description: Neoplastic fever is a noninfectious fever caused by inflammatory cytokine release from malignancy. It may occur in advanced or metastatic cancer and is a diagnosis of exclusion after infection and medication reactions are assessed.

case: 59-year-old man with history of prostate cancer metastatic to lumbar spine and periaortic lymph nodes diagnosed in 2001, with initial PSA of 11.3 ng/mL. In August 2011, presented to emergency room with abdominal pain. Lab tests showed elevated lipase (874 U/L), alkaline phosphatase (289 IU/L), and ALT (222 IU/L), with normal bilirubin. Later returned with right upper quadrant abdominal pain, tachycardia but afebrile. Physical exam showed positive Murphy's sign and palpable gallbladder. Labs showed elevated alkaline phosphatase of 357 IU/L and normal serum lipase.

Acute calculous cholecystitis.description: Inflammation of the gallbladder, usually caused by obstruction of the cystic duct by a gallstone.

Gallstone pancreatitis.description: Acute pancreatitis caused by transient or persistent obstruction of the pancreaticobiliary system by a gallstone.

Choledocholithiasis.description: Presence of gallstones in the common bile duct, which can cause biliary pain and abnormal liver enzyme levels and may precipitate pancreatitis or cholecystitis.

Acute acalculous cholecystitis.description: Gallbladder inflammation without gallstones, often occurring in critically ill patients or in the setting of malignancy, systemic illness, or impaired gallbladder emptying.

case: 13-year-old boy with a history of bilateral cryptorchidism, inguinal hernia, hypospadias, deficient tear production since infancy, developmental delay with mild intellectual disability, and isolated Addison’s disease diagnosed at age 4 after recurrent vomiting, failure to thrive, hyperpigmentation, hypotonia, hypoglycemia, and hypothermia. He later developed progressive muscle weakness, excessive fatigue, severe dysphagia beginning at age 11, and recent gait ataxia. Examination showed severe hyperpigmentation and hyperkeratosis of the elbows and knuckles, facial dysmorphism, dysarthria, nasal speech, saccadic eye movements with horizontal gaze nystagmus, dilated pupils with poor light response, mild bilateral optic atrophy, distal arm muscle wasting and weakness, milder pyramidal weakness in the legs, unsteady gait, hyperreflexia, and bilateral extensor plantar responses. Labs showed markedly elevated ACTH with normal electrolytes, aldosterone, and renin; very long chain fatty acids were normal.

Allgrove syndrome (Triple A syndrome / 4.normalized_text: Allgrove syndrome (Triple A syndrome / 4A syndrome with neurologic involvement)
Allgrove syndrome (Triple A syndrome / 4.description: A rare autosomal recessive disorder, usually caused by AAAS gene variants, characterized by alacrima, achalasia, ACTH-resistant primary adrenal insufficiency, and progressive autonomic and neurologic dysfunction. The neurologic form is sometimes called 4A syndrome.

X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy.description: A peroxisomal disorder caused by ABCD1 gene variants that can produce primary adrenal insufficiency and progressive neurologic disease, including spasticity, ataxia, cognitive decline, and optic pathway involvement.

Familial glucocorticoid deficiency.description: A group of inherited disorders of ACTH resistance causing isolated cortisol deficiency with high ACTH concentrations, hyperpigmentation, hypoglycemia, recurrent illness, and normal mineralocorticoid function.

Adrenal hypoplasia congenita.description: An inherited cause of primary adrenal insufficiency, often X-linked, that usually presents in boys with vomiting, hypoglycemia, poor growth, hyperpigmentation, and adrenal crisis; some forms can be associated with hypogonadotropic hypogonadism.

case: 55-year-old woman with a 13-year history of invasive ductal carcinoma of the right breast, stage IV with metastases to bone, lungs, and liver, status post mastectomy and multiple systemic therapies including stem-cell transplantation 8 years earlier; recently on anastrozole for 3 months and paracetamol for pain. She developed progressive generalized weakness and episodic confusion over several days, rapidly worsening to unresponsiveness. On admission she was found disoriented, with lower leg weakness and inability to follow basic instructions; exam showed awake but unresponsive and uncooperative, without focal neurologic deficits initially. Vitals were afebrile with normal blood pressure and mild tachycardia. Baseline brain MRI 2 weeks earlier was normal.

Hypercalcemic crisis due to metastatic b.normalized_text: Hypercalcemic crisis due to metastatic breast cancer
Hypercalcemic crisis due to metastatic b.description: Severe hypercalcemia, often from bone metastases or tumor-mediated parathyroid hormone-related peptide production, can cause acute encephalopathy, profound weakness, dehydration, cardiac arrhythmias, and coma.

Hepatic encephalopathy from liver metast.normalized_text: Hepatic encephalopathy from liver metastases or acute liver dysfunction
Hepatic encephalopathy from liver metast.description: Hepatic encephalopathy is impaired brain function caused by liver failure or extensive hepatic tumor involvement, leading to accumulation of neurotoxins such as ammonia and causing confusion, altered behavior, reduced consciousness, and coma.

Leptomeningeal carcinomatosis.description: Leptomeningeal carcinomatosis is spread of cancer cells to the meninges and cerebrospinal fluid. Breast cancer is a common cause and it may produce rapidly progressive confusion, weakness, cranial nerve deficits, seizures, and altered consciousness; an earlier normal brain MRI does not fully exclude it.

Nonconvulsive status epilepticus.description: Nonconvulsive status epilepticus consists of persistent seizure activity without obvious convulsions. It can present primarily with confusion, unresponsiveness, inability to follow commands, and fluctuating mental status, especially in patients with cancer or metabolic disturbances.

Acute toxic-metabolic encephalopathy.description: Toxic-metabolic encephalopathy is diffuse brain dysfunction caused by metabolic abnormalities, organ failure, medication effects, electrolyte disturbances, hypoglycemia, renal failure, or cancer-related systemic illness.

Brain metastases with cerebral edema.description: Brain metastases from breast cancer can cause cognitive changes, weakness, seizures, and reduced consciousness, particularly when lesions produce edema or increased intracranial pressure. However, a normal MRI 2 weeks earlier makes established large metastases less likely.

case: 54-year-old woman with no significant past medical history presented with 1 month of progressive weakness in all four extremities, sensory changes, and urinary difficulty. Exam showed increased deep tendon reflexes, bilateral positive Babinski, bilateral Hoffmann and Tromner signs, and asymmetric motor weakness (MRC 2 on the right, 4 on the left). Sensory loss was present below the C4 level, with decreased pinprick and temperature on the left and decreased vibration and proprioception on the right. Serologic autoimmune studies, CSF analysis, brain MRI, chest and abdominal CT, and nerve conduction study were unremarkable; angiotensin-converting enzyme was mildly elevated.

Neurosarcoidosis with spinal cord involv.description: Granulomatous inflammation from sarcoidosis can involve the spinal cord, causing subacute myelopathy, weakness, sensory deficits, and bladder dysfunction. Serum ACE may be elevated, although it is nonspecific.

Cervical intramedullary spinal cord tumo.description: An intramedullary tumor, such as ependymoma or astrocytoma, can gradually compress or infiltrate the cervical spinal cord and cause progressive myelopathy with long-tract signs and a sensory level.

Cervical spondylotic myelopathy.description: Degenerative narrowing of the cervical spinal canal can compress the spinal cord, producing upper motor neuron weakness, hand dysfunction, gait impairment, sensory changes, and bladder symptoms in advanced cases.

Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (.description: NMOSD is an autoimmune inflammatory disorder that can cause severe transverse myelitis, often involving long segments of the spinal cord and leading to weakness, sensory loss, and autonomic dysfunction.

Multiple sclerosis presenting as cervica.normalized_text: Multiple sclerosis presenting as cervical myelitis
Multiple sclerosis presenting as cervica.description: Multiple sclerosis can cause focal inflammatory demyelinating lesions in the cervical spinal cord, leading to weakness, sensory disturbances, hyperreflexia, and bladder dysfunction.

case: 33-year-old male with 20 days of cough and sputum production after a cold, with small amounts of yellow-white sticky sputum. No hemoptysis, fever, chills, dyspnea, or initial chest pain. He received intravenous treatment at a local clinic without improvement. Over the past 7 days, the cough worsened, especially at night causing sleep disturbance, sometimes with right-sided chest pain. Past history was unremarkable; he smoked about 10 cigarettes/day for over 10 years and did not drink alcohol. Physical examination showed T 36.2℃, P 112/min, R 19/min, BP 126/85 mmHg; symmetric chest, equal respiratory movement, symmetric vocal fremitus, clear bilateral percussion, coarse breath sounds in both lungs, and a small amount of wet rales in the right lung.

Acute bronchitis.description: Acute inflammation of the bronchi, usually following a viral upper respiratory infection, causing persistent cough with or without sputum production.

Community-acquired pneumonia.description: An infection of the lung tissue caused by bacteria, viruses, or atypical organisms; it can present with cough, sputum, focal crackles, and chest pain.

Postinfectious cough.description: A persistent cough caused by temporary airway inflammation and hypersensitivity after a resolved viral respiratory infection; it may last several weeks.

Cough-variant asthma or postviral bronch.normalized_text: Cough-variant asthma or postviral bronchial hyperresponsiveness
Cough-variant asthma or postviral bronch.description: Airway hyperreactivity that can be triggered by a respiratory infection and may present predominantly as persistent or nocturnal cough, sometimes without obvious wheezing.

Pertussis (whooping cough) in an adult.description: A Bordetella pertussis respiratory infection that can cause prolonged, severe, often nocturnal coughing episodes in adults, sometimes without the classic inspiratory whoop.

case: A 64-year-old male patient from Smoljanci, Istria presented with firm, migrating nodules in the brachial region without history of serious disease. He had no travel outside Croatia but spent recreational time in forests and islands near his residence and owned a pet dog. Physical examination revealed a painless, well-demarcated subcutaneous nodule in his right upper arm measuring 1.5 × 1.5 × 1.0 cm. Ultrasonographic findings of the nodule appeared normal. Laboratory tests showed total blood counts, erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein within normal values. Serologic results for trichinosis, toxocariasis, schistosomiasis, distomatosis and cysticercosis were negative.

Subcutaneous dirofilariasis (Dirofilaria.description: A zoonotic filarial infection transmitted by mosquitoes, commonly involving dogs as reservoir hosts. In humans, Dirofilaria repens can cause painless migrating subcutaneous nodules, particularly in Mediterranean countries including Croatia.

Subcutaneous sparganosis.description: A tissue infection caused by migrating larval tapeworms of Spirometra species. It can present as a painless, slowly migrating subcutaneous mass, although it is uncommon in Croatia.

Loiasis (Loa loa filarial infection).description: A filarial nematode infection that can cause transient migratory subcutaneous swellings known as Calabar swellings. It is endemic mainly in Central and West Africa and is transmitted by deer flies.

Onchocerciasis (Onchocerca volvulus infe.description: A filarial infection transmitted by blackflies that may produce firm subcutaneous nodules containing adult worms, often accompanied by skin and eye disease. It is primarily endemic in sub-Saharan Africa and limited areas of Latin America and Yemen.

Nodular fasciitis.description: A benign, rapidly growing reactive proliferation of fibroblasts that presents as a solitary, firm subcutaneous or intramuscular nodule, often on the upper extremities.

case: 66-year-old man with progressive gait instability and falls beginning around 2000, later developing blurred vision, photophobia, dysphagia, and repeated aspirations. He had bilateral cataract surgery with lens implantation in 2000 without improvement. Symptoms worsened over years with imbalance, unsteadiness, backward falls, slurred speech, inability to look down, and increasing swallowing difficulty. Exam showed irregular pupils with sluggish direct light reflexes, marked limitation of voluntary vertical and horizontal eye movements with preserved reflex eye movements early on, bilateral adduction paresis, later near-complete ophthalmoplegia with absent vertical and medial movements, impaired convergence, absent Bell’s phenomenon, optokinetic and caloric responses, and no doll’s eye movements. He also had severe nuchal rigidity, retrocollis, axial rigidity, inability to sit unsupported, and backward falling; reflexes were symmetric and mildly brisk with flexor plantar responses and no resting tremor.

Progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP), Ri.description: A progressive atypical parkinsonian neurodegenerative disorder characterized by early postural instability and falls, vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, axial rigidity, dysarthria, and dysphagia.

Niemann-Pick disease type C, adult-onset.normalized_text: Niemann-Pick disease type C, adult-onset form
Niemann-Pick disease type C, adult-onset.description: A lysosomal lipid-storage disorder that can present in adulthood with progressive neurologic decline, vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, ataxia, dysarthria, dystonia, psychiatric symptoms, and swallowing impairment.

Multiple system atrophy (MSA), parkinson.normalized_text: Multiple system atrophy (MSA), parkinsonian or cerebellar type
Multiple system atrophy (MSA), parkinson.description: A rapidly progressive neurodegenerative synucleinopathy causing autonomic failure, parkinsonism, cerebellar ataxia, dysarthria, dysphagia, and sometimes abnormal eye movements.

Corticobasal syndrome / corticobasal deg.description: An atypical parkinsonian syndrome with asymmetric rigidity, apraxia, cortical sensory deficits, dystonia, myoclonus, cognitive impairment, and occasionally supranuclear gaze palsy.

Brainstem neurodegenerative disorder or.normalized_text: Brainstem neurodegenerative disorder or structural midbrain disease causing supranuclear ophthalmoplegia
Brainstem neurodegenerative disorder or.description: Lesions affecting the midbrain and brainstem ocular motor networks, including neurodegenerative disease, tumors, vascular disease, inflammatory disease, or other infiltrative processes, can produce vertical gaze palsy, impaired convergence, dysphagia, and postural instability.

case: A 36-year-old man, sexually active with men, presented to the emergency department with a 2-week history of fever, headache, drowsiness, and photophobia. He was previously healthy. Physical examination revealed a temperature of 38.3°C and neck stiffness. CT of the head was normal. Lumbar puncture showed an opening pressure of 29 cm of water (ref: <20 cm). CSF analysis revealed: cell count 340 cells/µL (90% mononuclear cells, predominantly lymphocytes), glucose 46 mg/dL, and protein 0.80 g/L. HIV antibody test was positive with viral load 300,000 copies/mL and CD4+ count of 7 cells/µL.

Cryptococcal meningitis.description: Opportunistic fungal meningitis caused primarily by Cryptococcus neoformans, most common in patients with advanced HIV/AIDS and very low CD4 counts. It often causes subacute meningitis with elevated intracranial pressure.

Tuberculous meningitis.description: A subacute or chronic meningitis caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, often producing lymphocytic CSF inflammation, elevated protein, and increased opening pressure. Risk is increased in advanced HIV infection.

Viral (aseptic) meningitis or meningoenc.description: Meningitis caused by viruses such as herpes simplex virus, varicella-zoster virus, enteroviruses, or HIV itself. CSF usually shows lymphocytic pleocytosis with relatively preserved glucose.

Neurosyphilis (syphilitic meningitis).description: Central nervous system involvement by Treponema pallidum that can present as subacute meningitis, particularly in people with HIV. CSF often shows lymphocytic pleocytosis and elevated protein.

Acute bacterial meningitis.description: Meningitis caused by bacterial pathogens such as Streptococcus pneumoniae or Neisseria meningitidis. It typically presents acutely with fever, headache, photophobia, and meningeal irritation, but CSF usually has neutrophil predominance and lower glucose.

case: An 83-year-old woman presented to the acute stroke unit with sudden onset double vision that had lasted for three hours. She had a medical history of monoclonal gammopathy of uncertain significance and atrial fibrillation, for which she was not receiving anticoagulation because of an adverse reaction to warfarin. She had no history of transient ischaemic attack or stroke. She had diplopia only when looking through her right eye. On examination, she was unable to adduct her left eye, with nystagmus in her right eye when she attempted to do this. Her neurological examination was otherwise normal.

Ischemic internuclear ophthalmoplegia du.normalized_text: Ischemic internuclear ophthalmoplegia due to a medial longitudinal fasciculus infarction
Ischemic internuclear ophthalmoplegia du.description: A small brainstem ischemic stroke affecting the medial longitudinal fasciculus, producing impaired adduction of the ipsilateral eye and nystagmus of the abducting contralateral eye.

Posterior circulation ischemic stroke.description: An ischemic stroke involving the vertebrobasilar circulation, potentially affecting the pons or midbrain pathways responsible for coordinated eye movements.

Ocular myasthenia gravis.description: An autoimmune neuromuscular junction disorder that can cause fluctuating diplopia and ophthalmoplegia, often without limb weakness.

Multiple sclerosis causing internuclear.description: A demyelinating central nervous system disease that can affect the medial longitudinal fasciculus and produce internuclear ophthalmoplegia.

case: 35-day-old male infant with fever, vomiting, mottled skin, pallor, severe anemia, and respiratory distress. He was previously healthy, born at 37.5 weeks’ gestation as a fraternal twin by cesarean section for breech presentation, and fed breast milk plus formula. Two days before admission he was well; the day before he became fussy with pale, warm skin and one episode of vomiting; on admission he had worsening vomiting and tachycardia. At presentation he was febrile (39.1°C), tachycardic, tachypneic with retractions, pale, listless, and mottled, with a holosystolic-flow murmur and splenomegaly (2–3 cm below the costal margin). Urinalysis showed dark red, cloudy urine with blood, protein, and granular casts.

Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD).normalized_text: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency with acute hemolytic crisis
Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD).description: An inherited red-blood-cell enzyme deficiency, often X-linked, in which oxidative stress from infection, certain drugs, or foods can trigger sudden intravascular hemolysis.

Neonatal sepsis with disseminated intrav.normalized_text: Neonatal sepsis with disseminated intravascular coagulation and hemolysis
Neonatal sepsis with disseminated intrav.description: A severe systemic bacterial or viral infection in a young infant that can cause fever, poor feeding, vomiting, shock, respiratory distress, anemia, kidney injury, and coagulation abnormalities.

Autoimmune hemolytic anemia.description: A condition in which antibodies target red blood cells, causing rapid red-cell destruction; it may occur after infection and can cause severe anemia, jaundice, hemoglobinuria, and splenic enlargement.

Hereditary spherocytosis with hemolytic.description: An inherited red-blood-cell membrane disorder that causes chronic or intermittent hemolytic anemia, jaundice, splenomegaly, and worsening anemia during infections.

Hemolytic uremic syndrome or another thr.normalized_text: Hemolytic uremic syndrome or another thrombotic microangiopathy
Hemolytic uremic syndrome or another thr.description: A syndrome of red-cell destruction, low platelets, and acute kidney injury, often following infection; it can produce anemia, hematuria, proteinuria, and systemic illness.

case: 70-year-old man with history of Gleason 9 (4+5) adenocarcinoma treated with radical prostatectomy 10 years ago. Presented to primary care with rectal pain persisting for several weeks. Patient had lost 20 lbs over 3-4 weeks and complained of progressive fatigue, poor appetite, severe tenesmus, and rectal pain. Patient had been living independently on West Coast but relocated to East Coast to be closer to adult children.

Locally recurrent prostate adenocarcinom.normalized_text: Locally recurrent prostate adenocarcinoma with rectal invasion
Locally recurrent prostate adenocarcinom.description: Recurrence of high-grade prostate cancer after prostatectomy, potentially involving the prostate bed, pelvic tissues, or rectum and causing obstructive rectal symptoms.

Rectal adenocarcinoma.description: A malignant tumor arising in the rectum that can cause rectal pain, tenesmus, weight loss, fatigue, and appetite loss, particularly when locally advanced.

Metastatic prostate cancer.description: Disseminated recurrence of prostate adenocarcinoma after prior definitive treatment, which may produce constitutional symptoms and pelvic or rectal pain from local or metastatic disease.

Anal canal squamous cell carcinoma.description: A cancer of the anal canal that can cause anorectal pain, tenesmus, and constitutional symptoms when advanced.

Pelvic malignancy causing rectal compres.normalized_text: Pelvic malignancy causing rectal compression or invasion
Pelvic malignancy causing rectal compres.description: A pelvic tumor, including recurrent prostate cancer or another pelvic malignancy, can compress or invade the rectum and cause pain, tenesmus, and systemic cancer-related symptoms.

case: 27-year-old man with 3 days of progressive myalgias in the upper legs, followed by acute inability to lift his legs or stand on the day of presentation and new arm weakness. For several months, he had difficulty sleeping, loose stools, ~5 kg weight loss, and hand tremors. He had moved from El Salvador to Boston 5 months earlier and started an herbal supplement 4 days before presentation. On exam, he had bilateral conjunctival injection, proximal weakness in the upper and lower extremities, 3+ patellar reflexes, and a fine hand tremor. Labs showed severe hypokalemia, mild transaminitis, mild alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin elevation, elevated creatine kinase and aldolase, and venous pH 7.29.

Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis.description: An acute hypokalemic paralysis caused by intracellular potassium shifting in the setting of thyrotoxicosis, most often due to Graves disease. It commonly affects young men and causes sudden proximal leg weakness that can progress to arm weakness.

Graves disease with thyrotoxicosis.description: An autoimmune cause of hyperthyroidism characterized by excessive thyroid hormone production, often producing tremor, weight loss, heat intolerance, insomnia, diarrhea, hyperreflexia, and sometimes eye findings. It can precipitate thyrotoxic periodic paralysis.

Barium poisoning from an herbal suppleme.normalized_text: Barium poisoning from an herbal supplement
Barium poisoning from an herbal suppleme.description: Barium exposure can cause profound hypokalemia by shifting potassium into cells, resulting in acute muscle weakness or paralysis, gastrointestinal symptoms, and potentially cardiac arrhythmias. Contaminated herbal products have been reported as a source.

Familial hypokalemic periodic paralysis.description: A genetic skeletal-muscle channel disorder causing episodic weakness associated with low serum potassium, often triggered by carbohydrate intake, rest after exercise, stress, or certain medications.

Guillain-Barre syndrome.description: An acute immune-mediated polyradiculoneuropathy that usually causes progressive, symmetric ascending weakness and reduced or absent reflexes, sometimes after an infection.

case: A 70-year-old woman presented to the clinic for a routine examination. The patient reported that this mass had been present since birth. Her symptoms were minimal, with occasional difficulty cleaning the area and halitosis from entrapped food, but she was otherwise asymptomatic regarding the lesion.

Oral lymphangioma.description: A benign congenital malformation of lymphatic vessels that can present as a longstanding soft-tissue mass in the oral cavity, often involving the tongue, lips, or buccal mucosa.

Oral hamartoma.description: A benign developmental overgrowth of normal tissue components occurring in an abnormal arrangement; oral hamartomas may be congenital and remain asymptomatic for many years.

Dermoid cyst of the oral cavity.normalized_text: Dermoid cyst of the oral cavity
Dermoid cyst of the oral cavity.description: A benign congenital cyst containing skin-related structures that may occur in the floor of the mouth and persist for decades, often causing little discomfort unless large.

Oral lipoma.description: A benign tumor of mature fat cells that appears as a painless, slow-growing soft tissue mass in the mouth, although it is usually acquired rather than congenital.

Fibroma (oral irritation fibroma or cong.normalized_text: Fibroma (oral irritation fibroma or congenital fibrous lesion)
Fibroma (oral irritation fibroma or cong.description: A benign fibrous soft-tissue growth that is typically painless and may interfere with oral hygiene when located in an area prone to food retention.

case: A 52-year-old woman presented with a two-day history of lower back pain radiating into her left leg with associated leg weakness. She had a history of chronic back pain. Neurological examination revealed reduced power in her left leg (3/5), but was otherwise normal.

diagnoses.name: Intervertebral disc prolapse
diagnoses.icd11_title: Intervertebral disc degeneration without prolapsed disc with determinant

Lumbar disc herniation with radiculopath.description: Protrusion of an intervertebral disc in the lumbar spine can compress a nerve root, causing low back pain radiating down one leg and weakness in muscles supplied by that nerve.

Lumbar spinal stenosis.description: Narrowing of the lumbar spinal canal or nerve-root foramina can compress spinal nerves and produce back pain, leg pain, numbness, or weakness.

Degenerative lumbar spondylolisthesis.description: Forward displacement of one lumbar vertebra over another, often from degenerative joint and disc disease, may narrow nerve passages and cause radicular pain and weakness.

Cauda equina syndrome due to lumbar nerv.normalized_text: Cauda equina syndrome due to lumbar nerve compression
Cauda equina syndrome due to lumbar nerv.description: Severe compression of the lower spinal nerve roots, commonly from a large disc herniation, can cause leg weakness and requires urgent evaluation because it may lead to bladder, bowel, and sensory deficits.

Lumbar epidural abscess.description: An infection in the epidural space can compress spinal nerve roots or the spinal cord, causing back pain and progressive neurological deficits; it is a serious condition requiring prompt assessment.

case: A 52-year-old Korean man presented with a 1-month history of general weakness that was aggravated three days before his emergency room visit. Initial neurologic examination revealed disorientation of time, place, and person, attention deficit, immediate memory disturbance, dysarthria, weakness of bilateral upper extremities with increased deep tendon reflexes, and right hemiparetic gait. Blood work showed an elevated eosinophil count of 5,500/μL, representing 41% of total white blood cells. The patient's clinical history and basic examinations did not reveal any identifiable cause of hypereosinophilia, including parasitic infection, neoplasm, vasculitis, or allergy. Additionally, the patient had no prior clinical symptoms or signs suggesting Churg-Strauss syndrome, such as sinusitis or asthma. Cardiac enzymes were elevated with creatine kinase-MB at 7.3 ng/ml and troponin-I at 4.78 ng/ml. An echocardiogram revealed mild left ventricular inferior wall hypokinesia.

Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome (H.description: A disorder characterized by persistent marked eosinophilia with organ damage after secondary causes such as parasites, allergy, vasculitis, and malignancy have been excluded. It can affect the heart and nervous system through eosinophilic tissue infiltration or thromboembolism.

Eosinophilic myocarditis associated with.description: Inflammation and injury of the heart muscle caused by eosinophil infiltration, often occurring in hypereosinophilic syndrome and potentially causing myocardial dysfunction, elevated cardiac enzymes, arrhythmias, or thromboembolic complications.

Cerebral infarction or embolic encephalo.normalized_text: Cerebral infarction or embolic encephalopathy related to hypereosinophilic syndrome
Cerebral infarction or embolic encephalo.description: Central nervous system involvement in hypereosinophilic syndrome may result from eosinophil-mediated vascular injury or cardiac thromboembolism, producing multifocal ischemic strokes and cognitive or focal neurologic deficits.

Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyang.description: A systemic eosinophilic vasculitis that can affect the peripheral nervous system, heart, lungs, skin, kidneys, and gastrointestinal tract. It typically occurs in patients with asthma, allergic rhinitis, or chronic sinus disease.

case: A 44-year-old woman with a history of breast cancer presented with abnormal findings on 18-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography imaging. She had previously been diagnosed with breast cancer (T1N2M0, Stage IIIa, intraductal carcinoma, triple negative cancer) and had undergone adjuvant chemotherapy and radiation therapy after a right breast conserving surgery 2 years prior. She was a non-smoker with no specific occupational or environmental exposure to known carcinogens and had been taking tamoxifen after chemotherapy. Laboratory results revealed mild anemia (hemoglobin 11.4 mg/dL) and leucopenia (3,300/μL), with all other results within normal limits. Additional laboratory findings included an elevated angiotensin I-converting enzyme level of 101 U/L, and her purified protein derivative skin test for tuberculosis was negative. The biopsy sample was also negative for tuberculosis antigen-specific interferon gamma.

Sarcoidosis.description: A systemic granulomatous inflammatory disease characterized by noncaseating granulomas, often involving the lungs and mediastinal lymph nodes. It can cause increased FDG uptake on PET imaging and mimic cancer recurrence.

Metastatic recurrence of breast cancer.description: Recurrent breast cancer can spread to lymph nodes, lungs, bones, liver, or other organs and may appear as hypermetabolic lesions on FDG-PET imaging.

Tuberculosis.description: An infectious disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis that may produce granulomatous inflammation and FDG-avid lymph nodes or pulmonary lesions.

Lymphoma.description: A malignancy of lymphocytes that can cause FDG-avid lymphadenopathy, anemia, and leukopenia. It may occur independently of or rarely after prior cancer treatment.

Sarcoid-like reaction associated with ma.normalized_text: Sarcoid-like reaction associated with malignancy or cancer therapy
Sarcoid-like reaction associated with ma.description: A sarcoid-like reaction is the development of noninfectious granulomatous inflammation in lymph nodes or organs in patients with malignancy or following cancer treatment; it can closely resemble metastatic disease on PET imaging.

case: 78-year-old woman referred for anemia with elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate. She had 2 months of lethargy and easy fatigue. Past history: hypertension and hypercholesterolemia, treated with perindopril and atorvastatin. Examination was normal, with no organomegaly or lymphadenopathy; ECOG performance status 1. Blood tests showed hemoglobin 99 g/L, normal white cell and platelet counts, ESR 120 mm/h, mildly elevated creatinine 110 mmol/L, calcium 2.81 mmol/L, and LDH 333 U/L. Further studies showed elevated IgG kappa paraprotein (32 g/L), β₂-microglobulin 6.3 mg/L, free kappa light chains 1,400 mg/L, and kappa/lambda ratio 280. Urine Bence-Jones protein (kappa) was present, with normal 24-hour urine protein excretion. Vitamin D, parathyroid hormone, and alkaline phosphatase were normal.

Multiple myeloma (IgG kappa type).description: A malignant plasma-cell disorder characterized by monoclonal immunoglobulin production, bone marrow involvement, anemia, kidney dysfunction, hypercalcemia, and excess light chains.

Smoldering multiple myeloma.description: An asymptomatic precursor plasma-cell disorder with a substantial monoclonal protein and/or increased bone marrow plasma cells but without definite myeloma-defining organ damage.

Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined si.description: A common premalignant plasma-cell condition involving a small monoclonal protein without anemia, kidney injury, hypercalcemia, bone disease, or other attributable organ damage.

AL (light-chain) amyloidosis associated.normalized_text: AL (light-chain) amyloidosis associated with a plasma-cell dyscrasia
AL (light-chain) amyloidosis associated.description: A disorder in which monoclonal light chains form amyloid deposits that can damage the kidneys, heart, nerves, liver, and other organs; it may coexist with multiple myeloma.

case: 20-year-old male with 3-year bilateral breast enlargement without nipple discharge. Over the prior 4 years, he had polydipsia, increased fluid intake, and polyuria that had recently improved. He also reported blurred vision corrected with glasses, occasional post-exertion headaches, decreased facial hair growth, and recent constipation. Past history included generalized nocturnal tonic-clonic seizures and focal right leg seizures from ages 6–13, treated with carbamazepine until age 14. Physical examination showed minimal facial hair, small testes, bilateral breast enlargement without nipple retraction, masses, or discharge, a small posterior anal fissure, and a small coccygeal lump with central punctum.

Craniopharyngioma.description: A benign but locally aggressive suprasellar tumor arising near the pituitary stalk that can cause pituitary hormone deficiencies, diabetes insipidus, visual symptoms, headaches, and hypogonadism.

Pituitary macroadenoma with hypopituitar.description: A large pituitary adenoma can compress normal pituitary tissue and the optic pathways, producing hypogonadism, visual disturbance, headaches, hypothyroidism, and occasionally diabetes insipidus if the stalk is involved.

Suprasellar germinoma.description: An intracranial germ cell tumor involving the hypothalamus or pituitary stalk, often occurring in adolescents or young adults and commonly causing central diabetes insipidus, visual symptoms, and anterior pituitary hormone deficiencies.

Hyperprolactinemia due to prolactinoma.description: A prolactin-secreting pituitary adenoma can suppress gonadotropin release, causing hypogonadism, reduced facial hair, small testes, gynecomastia, headaches, and visual symptoms from mass effect.

Panhypopituitarism with central diabetes.description: Deficiency of multiple pituitary hormones, often from a hypothalamic-pituitary lesion, can cause central diabetes insipidus, central hypothyroidism, and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism.

case: A 50-year-old man with a history of injecting drug use presented to the emergency department with reduced level of consciousness and left arm weakness following five days of swinging fever, rigors, and headache. His past medical history included hepatitis C infection, paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, and a recent hospital admission for discitis and psoas abscess. On examination, his temperature was 38.4°C but he was hemodynamically stable and alert. Physical findings included a soft early diastolic decrescendo murmur along the left sternal border, splinter hemorrhages, a small digital infarct of the left third toe, and mild upper motor neuron pattern weakness in the left arm. Laboratory investigations revealed normocytic anemia and leukocytosis, with blood cultures growing methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus.

Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aur.description: Infection of the endocardial surface of the heart, usually involving a valve, caused here by MRSA. It can produce fever, new murmurs, persistent bacteremia, and embolic complications.

Aortic valve infective endocarditis with.normalized_text: Aortic valve infective endocarditis with aortic regurgitation
Aortic valve infective endocarditis with.description: Infective endocarditis affecting the aortic valve can damage the valve and cause a soft early diastolic decrescendo murmur consistent with aortic regurgitation. It may also cause systemic septic emboli.

Acute ischemic stroke due to septic embo.normalized_text: Acute ischemic stroke due to septic embolism
Acute ischemic stroke due to septic embo.description: A cerebral infarction caused by embolization of infected material from infective endocarditis. Septic emboli can produce focal neurological deficits and altered consciousness, often in the setting of fever and bacteremia.

Cardioembolic ischemic stroke related to.normalized_text: Cardioembolic ischemic stroke related to paroxysmal atrial fibrillation
Cardioembolic ischemic stroke related to.description: Paroxysmal atrial fibrillation can lead to thrombus formation in the heart and embolic stroke, causing sudden focal neurological deficits such as unilateral arm weakness.

case: 7-day-old female newborn born at full-term to a G1P1 mother with birth weight of 4,380 gm. Parents denied poor feeding, poor activity, or weak crying. On examination at Day 7, she had normal muscle power, normal reflex, no macroglossia, but slightly decreased facial folds. Newborn screening for Pompe disease showed GAA activity 0.18 uM/h (critical cutoff <0.5) and ratio 42.87 (critical cutoff acid β-glucosidase/GAA ≥20). Laboratory examination revealed elevated pro-BNP (8,738 pg/mL), CK (722 U/L), and ALT (112 U/L). Confirmatory testing showed deficient lymphocyte GAA activity (1.33 nmol/g pro/hr, normal mean 66.7). Patient did not have the common CRIM-positive Taiwan Pompe disease p.D645E variant. Mutation analysis revealed heterozygous c.2024_2026del (p.N675del) and c.2040+1G>T variants in trans.

Infantile-onset Pompe disease (glycogen.normalized_text: Infantile-onset Pompe disease (glycogen storage disease type II)
