Infantile-onset Pompe disease (glycogen.description: A lysosomal storage disorder caused by acid alpha-glucosidase (GAA) deficiency, leading to glycogen accumulation in cardiac, skeletal, and respiratory muscle. Classic infantile-onset disease commonly causes hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, hypotonia, and muscle weakness during early infancy.

Non-classic infantile Pompe disease.description: A less rapidly progressive form of Pompe disease in which residual GAA activity is present and severe cardiomyopathy may be absent or delayed. Muscle weakness and respiratory involvement can develop later in infancy or childhood.

Late-onset Pompe disease.description: A milder Pompe disease phenotype that usually presents in childhood or adulthood with progressive proximal muscle weakness and respiratory muscle weakness, typically without significant infantile cardiomyopathy.

Pompe disease with an initially asymptom.normalized_text: Pompe disease with an initially asymptomatic neonatal presentation
Pompe disease with an initially asymptom.description: A genetically and enzymatically confirmed Pompe disease state identified by newborn screening before overt clinical manifestations such as hypotonia, feeding difficulty, macroglossia, or cardiomyopathy become apparent.

case: 6-year-old girl with a 1-year history of intermittent migratory bone and joint pain, including left-hand pain after a fall, rib pain, right knee pain with limping, and left flank pain radiating to the left leg. Six days before admission, she developed back pain, limping, and intermittent fever up to 39.8°C. The day before admission, she developed periorbital swelling/discoloration, abdominal distention, and periumbilical discoloration. On examination, she was febrile (38.7°C), had bilateral periorbital discoloration, slight limping, and flinching with external rotation of the right hip; abdomen was soft and nontender. Past history included infant gastroesophageal reflux and pollen allergy with allergic rhinitis.

Neuroblastoma with metastatic bone marro.normalized_text: Neuroblastoma with metastatic bone marrow and skeletal involvement
Neuroblastoma with metastatic bone marro.description: A childhood cancer arising from sympathetic nervous system tissue, commonly in the adrenal glands or abdomen. Advanced disease can spread to bone and bone marrow, causing bone pain, limp, fever, abdominal enlargement, and characteristic periorbital ecchymosis ('raccoon eyes').

Acute lymphoblastic leukemia.description: A malignancy of immature lymphoid blood cells that commonly occurs in children. Bone marrow involvement can cause bone and joint pain, fever, limp, bruising or discoloration, and sometimes abdominal enlargement from liver or spleen enlargement.

Ewing sarcoma or disseminated Ewing sarc.normalized_text: Ewing sarcoma or disseminated Ewing sarcoma
Ewing sarcoma or disseminated Ewing sarc.description: A malignant bone or soft-tissue tumor most often affecting children and adolescents. It can cause persistent localized bone pain, swelling, limp, fever, and, when metastatic, symptoms from multiple bones or bone marrow involvement.

Acute hematogenous osteomyelitis or mult.normalized_text: Acute hematogenous osteomyelitis or multifocal osteomyelitis
Acute hematogenous osteomyelitis or mult.description: A bacterial infection of bone that can produce fever, localized bone pain, limp, and pain with movement of an adjacent joint. Multifocal disease is possible but less common.

Systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis.description: A childhood inflammatory arthritis that may cause intermittent high fever, joint pain, limp, and systemic inflammation. Some children have migratory symptoms before clear arthritis develops.

case: 54-year-old woman without comorbidities presented to emergency department with 12-hour history of redness and painful swelling in left gluteal region. Denied trauma. At admission: afebrile (36.2°C), normal blood pressure (109/65 mmHg), heart rate 89 bpm, mild peripheral oxygen desaturation (92% on room air) without respiratory distress. Rest of physical exam normal.

Cellulitis.description: A bacterial infection of the deeper layers of the skin and subcutaneous tissue, commonly causing localized redness, warmth, swelling, and tenderness.

Erysipelas.description: A superficial bacterial skin infection, usually caused by streptococci, characterized by painful red swelling that may have well-demarcated borders.

Gluteal abscess.description: A localized collection of pus within the skin or deeper soft tissues, often due to bacterial infection such as Staphylococcus aureus.

Necrotizing soft tissue infection.description: A rapidly progressive, life-threatening bacterial infection of fascia and soft tissues that can initially resemble cellulitis but typically causes severe pain and systemic toxicity.

Herpes zoster (shingles).description: Reactivation of varicella-zoster virus causing pain, burning, and a usually unilateral rash in a dermatomal distribution; the rash may begin with redness before vesicles appear.

case: 41-year-old white male with history of myelofibrosis. Past medical history includes splenectomy and allogeneic peripheral hematopoietic stem cell transplantation from single-antigen mismatched unrelated donor 2 years prior. After sun exposure during sailing trip, developed nonpruritic rash on face, trunk and extremities, associated with intermittent fever, muscle pain and weakness. Only current medication is daily oral acyclovir. Vital signs normal. Physical exam showed impaired ability to dorsiflex wrists while bringing palms together ('prayer sign'). Lab results showed: AST 41 U/L, ALT 68 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 147 U/L, total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL. Antinuclear antibody test positive (1:320) with speckled pattern.

Chronic graft-versus-host disease (cGVHD.normalized_text: Chronic graft-versus-host disease (cGVHD) with sclerodermatous/fascial involvement
Chronic graft-versus-host disease (cGVHD.description: A late complication of allogeneic stem cell transplantation in which donor immune cells attack recipient tissues. Skin and fascia involvement can cause sclerosis, reduced joint mobility, and the prayer sign.

Dermatomyositis.description: An autoimmune inflammatory myopathy characterized by proximal muscle weakness, muscle inflammation, and photosensitive skin manifestations; it may occur after transplantation or as an autoimmune-like manifestation of chronic GVHD.

Systemic sclerosis (scleroderma) or scle.normalized_text: Systemic sclerosis (scleroderma) or scleroderma-like chronic GVHD
Systemic sclerosis (scleroderma) or scle.description: A connective tissue disease involving skin thickening and fibrosis that can cause reduced hand and wrist mobility. A similar scleroderma-like syndrome can occur as a manifestation of chronic graft-versus-host disease.

Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) or lu.normalized_text: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) or lupus-like autoimmune syndrome after transplantation
Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) or lu.description: A multisystem autoimmune disease that can cause photosensitive rash, fever, myalgias, positive antinuclear antibodies, and liver test abnormalities. Lupus-like syndromes may rarely emerge after immune reconstitution or transplantation.

case: 51-year-old Caucasian male patient with terminal kidney disease presenting with a 10-month history of pruritic papules on sun-exposed areas of extremities. Patient suffered from severe pruritus with impaired sleep. Medical history includes arterial hypertension, hyperuricemia, coronary heart disease, terminal kidney disease due to idiopathic nephropathy, kidney transplants in 1990 and 2001 with rejections in 2000 and 2007, peritoneal dialysis from 2007-2017, ongoing hemodialysis since 2017, and factor V Leiden mutation. No history of habitual UV-light exposure or carcinogen exposure. Medications included felodipine, bisoprolol, clonidine, ramipril, urapidil, cholecalciferol, acetylsalicylic acid, allopurinol, phenprocoumon, thyroxine, iodine, fluvastatin, calcium acetate, omeprazole, and sevelamer carbonate.

Acquired perforating dermatosis (dialysi.normalized_text: Acquired perforating dermatosis (dialysis-associated perforating dermatosis, including acquired reactive perforating collagenosis/Kyrle disease)
Acquired perforating dermatosis (dialysi.description: A chronic pruritic skin disorder characterized by keratotic papules or nodules with transepidermal elimination of dermal material. It commonly occurs in patients with chronic kidney failure, diabetes, and long-term dialysis.

Prurigo nodularis.description: A chronic inflammatory skin condition with intensely itchy papules or nodules caused and maintained by repeated scratching. It may occur in association with systemic pruritus, including chronic kidney disease.

Chronic kidney disease-associated prurit.description: Persistent itching associated with advanced chronic kidney disease and dialysis. It may be generalized or localized and can substantially impair sleep and quality of life.

Porphyria cutanea tarda or dialysis-asso.normalized_text: Porphyria cutanea tarda or dialysis-associated pseudoporphyria
Porphyria cutanea tarda or dialysis-asso.description: Photosensitive blistering disorders that can cause fragile skin, erosions, crusts, milia, and sometimes pruritic lesions on sun-exposed areas. Pseudoporphyria may occur in patients receiving dialysis or certain medications.

Polymorphic light eruption.description: An immune-mediated photosensitivity eruption producing itchy papules, plaques, or vesicles after sun exposure, usually affecting exposed areas such as the arms and legs.

case: 15-year-old female with a history of ovarian cyst presented with left arm pain, frontal headaches, and conjunctival hyperaemia without fever or neurologic deficits. Seven days later, she developed acute lower back pain, left-sided paraesthesia, and left arm weakness. On admission, she had slight left-sided weakness, proximal pain in the left arm and leg worsened by movement, no fever, no meningism, and GCS 15. Labs showed leukocytosis and neutrophilia. By day 2, she developed dysuria, urinary retention, worsening left hemiparesis and pain, loss of temperature sensation below T2 on the left and T4 on the right, and bilateral Hoffman signs. CSF and electromyography were normal. Viral, bacterial, and autoimmune studies were negative except for high Zika virus PCR in serum, urine, and CSF.

Zika virus-associated acute transverse m.description: Inflammation of the spinal cord occurring after or during Zika virus infection, causing motor weakness, sensory-level abnormalities, pain, and autonomic dysfunction such as urinary retention.

Zika virus infection with neurologic com.normalized_text: Zika virus infection with neurologic complications
Zika virus infection with neurologic com.description: A mosquito-borne flavivirus infection that commonly causes conjunctivitis, headache, rash, fever, arthralgia, and may rarely cause central nervous system complications including myelitis or encephalomyelitis.

Acute partial transverse myelitis.description: A focal or asymmetric inflammatory spinal cord syndrome causing weakness, sensory deficits, pain, and bladder dysfunction; it may be infectious, post-infectious, autoimmune, or idiopathic.

Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (AD.description: An immune-mediated inflammatory demyelinating disorder of the brain and spinal cord that often follows a viral infection and can cause multifocal weakness, sensory abnormalities, and spinal cord dysfunction.

Guillain-Barre syndrome associated with.normalized_text: Guillain-Barre syndrome associated with Zika virus
Guillain-Barre syndrome associated with.description: An acute immune-mediated peripheral neuropathy that can follow Zika infection and typically causes progressive symmetric weakness, reduced reflexes, sensory symptoms, and sometimes autonomic dysfunction.

case: 27-year-old male presented with headache, dizziness, nausea, and vomiting for 3 days before admission. Physical examination showed no palpable lymph-node enlargement or hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory findings showed: WBC count 49.5×109/L, hemoglobin 161 g/L, platelet count 36×109/L, with 95% blasts in peripheral blood smear. Serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) was markedly elevated to 13,022 IU/L. Flow cytometry showed leukemic blasts were positive for CD2, CD7, CD5, and CD3, and negative for TdT, CD34, CD13, CD33, CD10, CD19, CD20, and CD22.

T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymp.normalized_text: T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma (T-ALL/LBL), mature immunophenotypic variant
T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymp.description: An aggressive hematologic malignancy of immature or precursor T cells, commonly affecting adolescents and young adults. Most cases express T-cell markers such as CD2, CD5, CD7, and cytoplasmic or surface CD3; TdT is usually positive but can be absent in rare mature-phenotype cases.

T-cell prolymphocytic leukemia (T-PLL).description: A rare mature T-cell leukemia characterized by marked lymphocytosis and expression of mature pan-T-cell markers, commonly CD2, CD3, CD5, and CD7. It usually occurs in older adults and often causes splenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, skin manifestations, and hepatomegaly.

Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATLL).description: A mature peripheral T-cell malignancy associated with human T-cell lymphotropic virus type 1 (HTLV-1). Leukemic ATLL can produce marked leukocytosis, circulating atypical T cells, high LDH, hypercalcemia, skin disease, lymphadenopathy, and organ involvement.

Peripheral T-cell lymphoma, not otherwis.normalized_text: Peripheral T-cell lymphoma, not otherwise specified, with leukemic peripheral blood involvement
Peripheral T-cell lymphoma, not otherwis.description: Peripheral T-cell lymphoma, not otherwise specified, is an aggressive mature T-cell neoplasm that may express variable pan-T-cell markers and can occasionally involve peripheral blood and bone marrow.

case: A 36-year-old Chinese man presented with a 1-month history of persistent fever. He was previously healthy with no significant past medical history, specifically no prior TB infections, chronic illnesses, liver or kidney disease, transfusions, malignancy, or immune diseases. He was not taking any regular prescription medications and had not travelled abroad. On admission, vital signs showed temperature 37.2°C, heart rate 119 beats/min, blood pressure 90/48 mmHg, respiration rate 38 breaths/min with oxygen saturation 88%. Physical examination revealed an acutely ill appearance and pulmonary rales in both lungs. He presented with persistent fever, pancytopenia, and hyperferritinemia with clinical deterioration including acute respiratory failure.

Secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocyt.description: A life-threatening hyperinflammatory syndrome caused by uncontrolled immune activation, commonly presenting with prolonged fever, cytopenias, very high ferritin levels, organ dysfunction, and respiratory deterioration.

Tuberculosis-associated hemophagocytic l.description: Secondary HLH triggered by active tuberculosis, often disseminated or miliary tuberculosis. It may cause persistent fever, pancytopenia, markedly elevated ferritin, pulmonary involvement, and multiorgan failure even without prior tuberculosis history.

Disseminated or miliary tuberculosis.description: A widespread form of tuberculosis resulting from hematogenous spread of Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It can produce prolonged fever, diffuse lung disease, cytopenias, respiratory failure, and may trigger secondary HLH.

Severe sepsis with acute respiratory dis.normalized_text: Severe sepsis with acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS)
Severe sepsis with acute respiratory dis.description: Severe systemic infection can cause fever, hypotension, tachycardia, tachypnea, cytopenias, respiratory failure, and inflammatory marker elevation. ARDS is a severe inflammatory lung injury causing hypoxemia and diffuse pulmonary findings.

Lymphoma-associated hemophagocytic lymph.description: Occult lymphoma, particularly T-cell or NK-cell lymphoma, can trigger HLH and cause prolonged fever, pancytopenia, hyperferritinemia, and rapidly progressive organ dysfunction.

case: An 81-year-old man presented to the ICU 10 days after a 4-week cruise in New Caledonia, Vanuatu, the Solomon Islands, and New Zealand. He was reported to have been in perfect health during the cruise. On examination, he was febrile (39.1°C) and comatose with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 6. He exhibited hemiplegia of the left side, paresis of the right upper limb, normal tendon reflexes, and a Babinski sign on the left side. A transient rash was observed within 48 hours of admission. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed leukocyte count of 41/mm³ (98% polymorphonuclear leukocytes), protein level of 76 mg/dL, and CSF:blood glucose ratio of 0.75.

Japanese encephalitis.description: A mosquito-borne flaviviral encephalitis occurring in parts of the Asia-Pacific region that can cause severe brain inflammation, coma, seizures, and focal neurologic deficits, particularly in older adults.

Dengue encephalitis.description: A neurologic complication of dengue virus infection in which direct viral brain involvement or severe systemic dengue causes altered consciousness, coma, focal deficits, and cerebrospinal fluid abnormalities.

Murray Valley encephalitis.description: A severe mosquito-borne flavivirus infection causing encephalitis, predominantly in Australia and nearby Oceania, with fever, impaired consciousness, coma, and neurologic deficits.

West Nile virus encephalitis.description: A mosquito-borne flaviviral infection that may cause severe encephalitis in older adults, with fever, confusion, coma, weakness, and focal neurologic abnormalities.

Acute bacterial meningitis or meningoenc.description: A bacterial infection of the meninges and brain, such as pneumococcal meningitis, that can cause high fever, coma, focal deficits, and neutrophil-predominant cerebrospinal fluid inflammation.

case: 20-year-old man with Crohn’s disease diagnosed at age 10, previously treated with prolonged glucocorticoids and improved over the past 3 years on weekly adalimumab, presented with 3 weeks of upper respiratory symptoms (sore throat, nonproductive cough, rhinorrhea, chills). Two weeks before presentation, he developed cramping left calf pain that worsened over 2 days, with swelling extending from the calf to the foot and a purpuric/erythematous rash on the dorsum of both feet. He also reported multiple prior self-limited episodes of similar upper respiratory symptoms. On examination, he was uncomfortable due to left leg pain, had left ankle synovitis, intact nasal septum, and normal peripheral pulses.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA).description: A small- and medium-vessel ANCA-associated vasculitis that can cause upper respiratory tract inflammation, skin purpura, arthritis, pulmonary disease, renal disease, and venous thrombosis.

IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura.description: An immune-complex small-vessel vasculitis often triggered by an upper respiratory infection, characterized by palpable purpura, joint pain or arthritis, abdominal symptoms, and possible kidney involvement.

Deep venous thrombosis (DVT).description: A blood clot in a deep vein, usually in the leg, causing unilateral pain, swelling, warmth, and risk of pulmonary embolism. Crohn’s disease and systemic inflammation increase thrombotic risk.

Adalimumab-associated leukocytoclastic v.description: A drug-induced small-vessel vasculitis that can occur with TNF-alpha inhibitors such as adalimumab and commonly presents with purpura on the lower extremities, arthralgia, and occasionally systemic involvement.

Erythema nodosum with peripheral arthrit.normalized_text: Erythema nodosum with peripheral arthritis related to Crohn’s disease
Erythema nodosum with peripheral arthrit.description: An extraintestinal manifestation of inflammatory bowel disease in which painful inflammatory skin lesions and peripheral arthritis, often involving the ankles, can occur during intestinal or systemic inflammation.

case: A 47-year-old man presented to his primary care physician with a six-month history of left-sided sore throat, ipsilateral otalgia, and a six-week history of a left-sided neck mass. He had never smoked and drank less than 5 units of alcohol per week. On examination in the ENT clinic, a firm fixed lymph node was palpable in the upper anterior triangle.

Human papillomavirus-associated orophary.normalized_text: Human papillomavirus-associated oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma
Human papillomavirus-associated orophary.description: A cancer of the tonsil or base of tongue often associated with HPV infection. It commonly occurs in nonsmokers and may first present with a painless or firm cervical lymph node metastasis.

Tonsillar squamous cell carcinoma.description: A malignant tumor arising from the palatine tonsil, often causing persistent unilateral throat pain, referred ear pain, and spread to upper cervical lymph nodes.

Base of tongue squamous cell carcinoma.normalized_text: Base of tongue squamous cell carcinoma
Base of tongue squamous cell carcinoma.description: A malignancy arising at the tongue base, frequently associated with HPV and often presenting with vague throat discomfort, referred otalgia, and cervical lymphadenopathy.

Nasopharyngeal carcinoma.description: A cancer of the nasopharynx that can present with upper cervical lymph node enlargement and referred ear symptoms; nasal or hearing symptoms may also occur.

Cervical lymphoma.description: Lymphoma can cause enlarged cervical lymph nodes and occasionally throat discomfort due to lymphoid tissue involvement in the tonsils or Waldeyer ring.

case: 72-year-old white woman with 10-year history of recurrent cystitis. No systemic symptoms. Physical exam showed slight anemia. Urine cultures were positive for Escherichia coli. No hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy detected by CT and ultrasound. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy and subsequent biopsies were negative for both pathologic lymphoid infiltrate and Helicobacter pylori. Otolaryngologic examination and bone marrow biopsy were negative. Serology for hepatitis C virus and hepatitis B virus was negative. No monoclonal component found in serum protein electrophoresis.

Primary urinary bladder extranodal margi.normalized_text: Primary urinary bladder extranodal marginal zone B-cell lymphoma of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT lymphoma)
Primary urinary bladder extranodal margi.description: A rare indolent B-cell lymphoma arising in the bladder, often associated with longstanding chronic cystitis or recurrent urinary tract infections and usually localized at diagnosis.

Chronic recurrent bacterial cystitis.description: Repeated lower urinary tract infection, commonly caused by Escherichia coli, which can produce persistent bladder inflammation over many years.

Follicular cystitis.description: A benign chronic inflammatory bladder condition characterized by lymphoid follicle formation, often associated with recurrent urinary tract infections and chronic irritation.

Primary diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of.normalized_text: Primary diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of the urinary bladder
Primary diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of.description: A rare aggressive bladder lymphoma that may arise in the setting of chronic cystitis but usually has a more rapidly progressive clinical course than MALT lymphoma.

case: 95-year-old woman admitted after a fall. Medical history includes Alzheimer's disease, hypertension, and type 2 diabetes mellitus (on metformin). Laboratory findings showed elevated white cell count and C reactive protein levels. Urine culture revealed Klebsiella pneumoniae infection. Blood cultures were negative.

Complicated urinary tract infection due.normalized_text: Complicated urinary tract infection due to Klebsiella pneumoniae
Complicated urinary tract infection due.description: A bacterial infection of the urinary tract caused by Klebsiella pneumoniae; in older adults it may present atypically with functional decline or falls rather than urinary complaints.

Acute pyelonephritis.description: An upper urinary tract infection involving the kidneys, usually causing systemic inflammation and often associated with fever, flank pain, and urinary symptoms.

Asymptomatic bacteriuria.description: The presence of bacteria in the urine without clear urinary tract symptoms; it is common in older adults and does not always represent a symptomatic infection.

Urosepsis.description: A systemic inflammatory response to a urinary tract infection that can cause organ dysfunction, confusion, weakness, hypotension, or falls, particularly in frail older adults.

case: 22-year-old athletic male presented with swelling and locking of the left knee. He had no recent trauma but had several football injuries as a child. Two years prior, he had experienced disabling knee pain.

Osteochondritis dissecans of the knee.description: A condition in which a segment of cartilage and underlying bone, often on the femoral condyle, becomes damaged and may partially or completely detach, creating a loose fragment in the knee joint.

Meniscal tear, including a bucket-handle.normalized_text: Meniscal tear, including a bucket-handle tear
Meniscal tear, including a bucket-handle.description: A tear of the knee meniscus can cause pain, recurrent swelling, catching, and mechanical locking, particularly when a displaced fragment blocks joint movement.

Intra-articular loose body of the knee.normalized_text: Intra-articular loose body of the knee
Intra-articular loose body of the knee.description: A free fragment of cartilage or bone within the knee joint, often resulting from osteochondritis dissecans, prior injury, or cartilage damage, can intermittently obstruct movement.

Synovial chondromatosis.description: A rare benign joint disorder in which the synovium forms multiple cartilage nodules that can detach into the joint as loose bodies, causing swelling, pain, and locking.

case: 48-year-old male presented with 1-week history of jaundice, dark brown urine, pale stools, and nausea. Medical history and physical exam were unremarkable. Laboratory findings showed hepatic panel in cholestatic pattern: total bilirubin 117 μmol/L, conjugated bilirubin 66.8 μmol/L, alkaline phosphatase 173 IU/L, γ-Glutamyltransferase 380 IU/L, Alanine transaminase 468 IU/L. CA19-9 was 11783 IU/mL. Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and β2-microglobulin were normal.

diagnoses.name: Primary pancreatic T-cell/histiocyte-rich large B-cell lymphoma
diagnoses.normalized_text: Primary pancreatic T-cell/histiocyte-rich large B-cell lymphoma

Pancreatic adenocarcinoma (pancreatic he.description: A malignant tumor of the pancreas, especially the head of the pancreas, that can obstruct the common bile duct and cause painless obstructive jaundice. CA19-9 can be markedly elevated.

Cholangiocarcinoma.description: Cancer of the bile ducts that commonly presents with biliary obstruction, jaundice, pale stools, dark urine, and elevated cholestatic liver enzymes. CA19-9 may be substantially elevated.

Choledocholithiasis (common bile duct st.description: A gallstone within the common bile duct can cause extrahepatic biliary obstruction, resulting in jaundice, dark urine, pale stools, nausea, and cholestatic liver test abnormalities. CA19-9 can occasionally rise markedly in benign obstruction.

Ampullary carcinoma.description: A malignancy arising at the ampulla of Vater can obstruct both the bile duct and pancreatic duct, causing obstructive jaundice. CA19-9 may be elevated.

Primary biliary lymphoma or secondary ly.normalized_text: Primary biliary lymphoma or secondary lymphomatous involvement of the biliary tract
Primary biliary lymphoma or secondary ly.description: Lymphoma can rarely involve the bile ducts, pancreas, porta hepatis, or liver and produce obstructive jaundice that can mimic pancreatic or biliary carcinoma. Normal LDH and beta-2 microglobulin do not completely exclude lymphoma.

case: 80-year-old woman with 6-month history of slowly increasing asymptomatic lumbar subcutaneous mass. History of chronic renal failure requiring dialysis three times weekly for 10 years. Poor compliance with phosphate-binding medications and dietary restrictions. Physical exam showed firm, immobile subcutaneous nodule measuring 9 cm in major axis. Laboratory findings: serum calcium 1.95 mmol/L (normal: 2.05-2.55), serum phosphorus 3.3 mmol/L (normal: 0.74-1.52), serum intact parathyroid hormone 142 ng/L (normal: 10-65), serum creatinine 787 μmol/L (normal: 53-106).

Uremic tumoral calcinosis.description: A periarticular or subcutaneous deposition of calcium-phosphate material occurring in patients with chronic renal failure, usually associated with hyperphosphatemia and secondary hyperparathyroidism.

Metastatic calcinosis cutis due to chron.normalized_text: Metastatic calcinosis cutis due to chronic kidney disease
Metastatic calcinosis cutis due to chron.description: Calcium salt deposition in skin and subcutaneous tissue caused by abnormal calcium-phosphate metabolism, often in end-stage renal disease with hyperphosphatemia and secondary hyperparathyroidism.

Calcified chronic hematoma.description: A chronic organized hematoma that may become firm or calcified over time, often after trauma, surgery, anticoagulation, or repeated minor injury.

Epidermoid cyst.description: A benign keratin-filled cyst arising from the epidermis or hair follicle, usually presenting as a slow-growing subcutaneous nodule.

Tophaceous gout.description: Deposition of monosodium urate crystals in soft tissues, producing firm nodules called tophi; chronic kidney disease can predispose to hyperuricemia and gout.

case: 47-year-old female presented to emergency department after being hit while skiing by another skier at high speed from behind. Immediate pain and marked general swelling of the knee joint occurred after impact. Unable to bear weight. Physical exam showed neurovascularly intact limb with no broken skin. No relevant medical, family, or social history.

Tibial plateau fracture.description: A fracture of the upper surface of the tibia involving the knee joint, often caused by high-energy impact and commonly associated with swelling and inability to bear weight.

Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tear.description: A tear of the anterior cruciate ligament, a major stabilizing ligament of the knee, usually caused by twisting, hyperextension, or high-force trauma.

Posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) tear.description: A tear of the posterior cruciate ligament, often resulting from a direct blow to the front of a flexed knee or other high-energy knee trauma.

Patellar fracture.description: A fracture of the kneecap caused by direct impact or forceful contraction of the quadriceps, producing anterior knee pain, swelling, and impaired weight bearing.

Knee dislocation with spontaneous reduct.description: A temporary displacement of the tibiofemoral joint that may reduce before examination; it is a high-energy injury that can involve multiple ligaments and carries a risk of vascular injury.

case: A 52-year-old woman presented with complaints of anal pain, constipation, and tenesmus for 3 months before being referred to the hospital. There were no relevant prior illnesses. Rectal digital examination revealed a 6-cm smooth elastic mass on the rectal posterior left side 2 cm from the anal verge. Colonoscopy showed a rectal submucosal bulging. Computed tomography scan and magnetic resonance imaging confirmed the presence of a single 6-cm well-delimited mass, compressing and infiltrating the wall of the medium to low rectum.

diagnoses.icd11_title: Gastrointestinal stromal tumour of unspecified gastrointestinal sites

Rectal gastrointestinal stromal tumor (G.description: A mesenchymal tumor arising from the gastrointestinal wall, most often from the muscular layer. Rectal GISTs commonly appear as well-circumscribed submucosal masses and may cause local compression or invasion.

Rectal leiomyoma.description: A benign smooth-muscle tumor that can arise from the muscularis propria of the rectum. It typically produces a smooth, submucosal, well-defined mass and may cause obstructive symptoms when large.

Rectal leiomyosarcoma.description: A rare malignant smooth-muscle tumor of the rectum. It can present as a growing intramural or submucosal mass with pain, bowel obstruction, and invasion of surrounding rectal tissues.

Rectal schwannoma.description: A rare nerve-sheath tumor arising in the gastrointestinal tract. Most rectal schwannomas are benign and present as slow-growing, well-circumscribed submucosal masses that can cause obstructive symptoms.

Rectal endometriosis.description: Endometriosis involving the rectum or rectovaginal region can form an infiltrative mass and cause pain, constipation, and tenesmus, usually in women of reproductive age and often with menstrual symptom variation.

case: Two-year-four-month-old female with IUGR at birth (39 weeks, C-section for placental failure; birth weight 1850 g, length 44.5 cm, head circumference 31 cm, all 3rd percentile). At 3 months, evaluated for hearing loss; ABR showed bilateral severe sensorineural hearing loss, and hearing aids were placed at 4 months. During infancy, she had persistent growth delay with weight and height below the 3rd percentile, but normal psychomotor development (sat at 8 months, walked at 14 months, talked at 13 months). CNS MRI was normal. Genetic testing identified a de novo heterozygous PIK3R1 variant c.1956dupT (p.Lys653*) in exon 15.

SHORT syndrome (PIK3R1-related SHORT syn.description: A rare autosomal dominant disorder caused by pathogenic PIK3R1 variants, characterized by prenatal and postnatal growth restriction, short stature, partial lipodystrophy, characteristic facial features, insulin resistance, and sometimes ocular or dental abnormalities. The identified de novo truncating PIK3R1 variant is strongly consistent with this diagnosis.

3-M syndrome.description: A genetic primordial growth disorder characterized by severe prenatal and postnatal growth restriction, low birth weight, short stature, and generally normal intelligence. It is usually caused by biallelic variants in CUL7, OBSL1, or CCDC8 rather than PIK3R1.

Silver-Russell syndrome.description: A growth disorder characterized by prenatal and postnatal growth restriction, low birth weight, short stature, feeding difficulties, and distinctive facial features. It is most often associated with abnormalities involving chromosome 11p15 or maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 7.
